2. It is information that circulates, spreading from person to person, rather than direct knowledge. The word evokes less the fact itself than the news that circulates about it.
3. The biblical context emphasizes information concerning disorder or crime: the tribune learns through this news that a riot is spreading through the city. It is urgent information that triggers action.
G5334.origine: The word comes from the verb phainoô ("to show, appear, shine"). Phasis originally designated what is shown or becomes visible, then the information that manifests itself, appearing to the one who receives it. In the Greek Old Testament, the word is used to translate news or denunciation reported to the authorities.
G5334.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:31. Paul is attacked at the temple in Jerusalem: as the crowd seeks to kill him, a rumor — a "false information" in a sense — reaches the Roman tribune. This news informs him that the entire city is in turmoil, prompting him to intervene quickly with his troops. It is a key moment: the news diverts attention from Paul himself and changes the course of events.
G5334.portee: This word reminds us of the power of information and communication. A simple piece of news, true or distorted, can dramatically change a situation. In Acts 21, it is this news that saves Paul's life by diverting the crowd's violence towards urban disorder. For the Christian reader, this underscores how God controls circumstances and even rumors to accomplish His purposes.

sens: To assert strongly that something is true
To claim something, to boast about it
G5335.detail:
1. To affirm is to declare with assurance and insistence that something is true or real. It is more than simply saying: it is giving testimony, taking a stand. When the Jews join in the accusation against Paul (Acts 24:9), they strongly affirm that the charges against him are just. It is a solid assertion from people taking a position.
2. The word can also mean to claim something, to attribute it to oneself, to boast — even when it is false or exaggerated. When men boast (Romans 1:22) of being wise, they affirm having a wisdom they do not truly possess. It is excessive confidence in one's own merits or knowledge.
G5335.origine: The verb comes from a Greek root meaning "to speak," "to say clearly." It expresses the idea of producing a sound, making a public declaration. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb "to say" (אָמַר), particularly when it involves affirming something with authority or conviction. The word has retained this nuance of solid and visible assertion.
G5335.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always in a context where someone takes a stand or claims something. In Acts, it designates the solid affirmation of the accusers against Paul (24:9) and Paul's own testimony affirming the resurrection of Jesus (25:19). In the letter to the Romans, it characterizes the vain claim of men who boast of a wisdom they do not have (1:22). It is always a public and visible word, never a secret thought.
G5335.portee: This word reminds us of the power of testimony: to affirm the truth of the Gospel is to take a public stand, as Paul did before the authorities. It also invites us to prudence: to guard against claiming a wisdom or righteousness that we do not truly possess, but which only the grace of Christ gives us.

sens: To not harm someone or something; to preserve them from danger or suffering
To refrain from inflicting a punishment that one has the right or power to impose
To hold back, to abstain from doing something out of consideration for others
G5339.detail:
1. Spare primarily means to refuse to cause harm to someone one could reach: the wolves "will not spare the flock" (Acts 20:29), meaning they will devour it mercilessly. It also means to preserve someone from a trial, as Paul wants to "spare" the Corinthians from tribulations (1 Corinthians 7:28).
2. To spare can mean to refuse to punish, even when one has the strength or the right: God "did not spare" His own Son, meaning He delivered Him to death (Romans 8:32); He "did not spare" the natural branches, having cut them off (Romans 11:21).
3. To abstain means to voluntarily hold back for the sake of others: Paul abstains from boasting "so that no one may think of me beyond what is in accordance with the truth" (2 Corinthians 12:6), he holds back out of regard for those who might be misled.
G5339.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of restraint and moderation. The same family contains words related to frugality and preservation. In Hebrew, the translated word is primarily חָמַל (hammal), which means to have pity or compassion, to show mercy towards one who could be struck.
G5339.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul’s writings and the apostles' epistles. Paul uses it to speak of God's relationship with His creatures (Romans 8:32, 11:21): God spares or does not spare according to His plan. Paul also uses it to describe his own pastoral attitude: he spares or abstains from the Corinthians out of love (2 Corinthians 1:23, 12:6). The word also appears to describe the danger posed by false teachers who will not spare the flock (Acts 20:29) and to express that God did not spare the angels who sinned (2 Peter 2:4-5).
G5339.portee: This word reminds Christians that God's grace is never a weakness: God "did not spare" His own Son shows that divine love is a force that acts in both judgment and mercy. For the disciple, to spare reflects a virtue: it is to exercise restraint and compassion towards those who might suffer from our words or actions, a mark of spiritual maturity.

sens: In small quantity, moderately
With restraint, without generosity
By extension, in a stingy or miserly manner
G5340.detail:
1. The word describes an action done in small quantity or with moderation. In 2 Corinthians 9:6, Paul uses it to speak of one who "sows little": the image of the sower shows that giving little results in reaping little — generosity towards others produces its fruits according to the measure one puts in.
2. Beyond simple quantity, the word carries the idea of restraint and frugality: one who acts "little" acts without fully committing, holding back, remaining in voluntary limitation.
3. In Paul’s context, "little" evokes fear, stinginess, or hesitation: it is the attitude opposite to the joyful liberality that characterizes true Christian giving.
G5340.origine: The word comes from a verb that means "to spare" or "to save," hence the image of a person who holds back, who only spends or gives moderately. This root refers to the idea of fear or restraint: one who acts "little" is one who fears, who lacks confidence or generosity. The word is formed like an adverb from a participle (a verbal form).
G5340.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:6. Paul uses it in his teaching on generosity towards the poor in Jerusalem. He states a spiritual law: he who sows little will reap little. This passage shows that "little" is not simply a neutral quantity, but a refusal to invest, to truly give. The apostle wants to awaken the Corinthians to a generosity that does not calculate, that does not hold back.
G5340.portee: This word reminds Christians that God observes our generosity and our heart in giving. To give "little" out of fear or stinginess impoverishes our own spiritual harvest. Conversely, giving abundantly with joy produces an abundance of blessings. It is an invitation to examine our motivations: do we reap little because we sow little?

sens: An outer garment, loose-fitting and sleeveless, thrown over the shoulders for protection against cold or rain
G5341.detail: 1. The word designates a practical garment for protection against bad weather, worn over other clothes. It is a Roman cloak called paenula in Latin, ample and draped, which is put on over the head. In the only biblical usage, Paul asks Timothy to bring the cloak he left in Troas, probably because he is cold during his captivity (2 Timothy 4:13).
G5341.origine: The Greek word comes from a Latin form (paenula) and has undergone several spelling variations in ancient manuscripts (phélonès, phailonès, phénolès). It simply designates a travel or bad weather garment, with no particular Hebrew origin since it is a word borrowed from Latin and Roman culture.
G5341.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:13. Paul, imprisoned in Rome at the end of his life, asks his young collaborator Timothy to bring him the cloak he left in Troas during a previous visit. The context suggests that Paul needs warm clothing, which shows us that even great apostles suffered from the cold and had concrete material needs. This simple mention of a daily object makes the narrative vivid and grounded in reality.
G5341.portee: This passage reminds us that material needs — to dress, to be warm — are legitimate and human, even for a servant of God as exemplary as Paul. It also shows the practical importance of brotherly help: Timothy must think of the concrete needs of the one who trained him. It is a lesson in simplicity and solidarity within the body of Christ.

sens: To physically carry something or someone from one place to another
To support the weight or burden of something
To endure, to bear suffering or difficulties
To produce, to generate (referring to fruits or results)
To lead, to guide someone somewhere
To present, to produce before someone (an accusation, a testimony)
G5342.detail:
1. To bear means to physically carry: to bring an object, to lead a person to a place or to another person. In Luke 15:23, the fattened calf is brought to the table. In Mark 8:22, a blind man is brought to Jesus. It is the concrete movement of bringing something from one place to another.

2. To bear can also mean to support, to hold the weight of a burden. The Son in Hebrews 1:3 bears the universe by His word — He continually supports it. It is less about movement and more about a responsibility maintained.

3. To bear means to endure, to support without complaint: in Hebrews 12:20, the Israelites could not bear the command that if a beast touched the mountain, it would be stoned. In Romans 9:22, God bears with patience vessels of wrath.

4. To bear fruit means to produce, to generate: a branch that bears fruit (John 15:8), a seed that bears many seeds (John 12:24). The fruit is what the heart naturally produces.

5. To bear someone also means to lead, to guide: in Acts 14:13, sacrifices are brought to the altars. In John 21:18, Peter will be led where he does not want to go — to be led forcefully.

6. To bear an accusation or a judgment means to present it, to produce it: in John 18:29, the Jews did not bring any specific accusation against Jesus. In 2 Peter 2:11, the angels do not bring a railing judgment.
G5342.origine: The verb φέρω is very ancient in Greek. It often translates the Hebrew נָשָׂא (nasâ), which means to lift, take, support. It can also translate בּוֹא (bô), to enter or come. The root suggests the idea of movement and transport: something that moves, shifts, carries. The verb is linked to a very concrete semantic background: the weight one lifts, the burden one carries, the path one travels.
G5342.emploi: This verb is used 60 times in the New Testament, in all the Gospels, in Acts, and in the epistles. In Mark and Luke, it is mainly used to report how the sick were brought to Jesus (Mark 1:32, 2:3, Luke 5:18). In the Gospels of John, it takes on a higher theological dimension: the Son bears the universe, believers bear fruit. In Acts, to bear means to bring gifts to the apostles (5:2). In the epistles, the meaning refines: to bear a moral burden (Hebrews 12:20), to bear the shame of Christ (Hebrews 13:13), to bear fruit in the Christian life (John 15). The same verb thus encompasses both concrete action and spiritual reality.
G5342.portee: To bear fruit calls Christians to produce a life worthy of the Gospel: love, justice, perseverance. To bear burdens — suffering, weakness, accusations — is to walk in the footsteps of Jesus and the cross. Understanding that the Son bears the universe strengthens trust in His governance. It is a word that unites daily concrete action with the deepest spiritual vocation.

sens: To run away quickly to escape danger or an immediate threat
To leave a place hastily, to abandon one's position
To evade, to distance oneself from someone or something
Figuratively: to resolutely avoid sin, temptation, or moral evil
To escape the authority or control of someone
G5343.detail:
1. To run away quickly to escape danger or an immediate threat: this is the most direct meaning of the verb. Joseph flees to Egypt to save the child Jesus from Herod's persecution (Matthew 2:13). During His ministry, Jesus Himself leaves a place when the time has not yet come (John 10:12).

2. To leave a place hastily, to abandon one's position: the disciples flee after Jesus' arrest (Mark 14:50), and Mark reports that the young man who followed Jesus "fled" naked, leaving his garment behind (Mark 14:52). This is a panic flight, without calculation.

3. To evade, to distance oneself from someone or something: the sheep flee from the thief because they do not recognize his voice (John 10:5). Here, the verb expresses an instinctive distancing, a mistrust.

4. Figuratively: to resolutely avoid sin, temptation, or moral evil: Paul instructs the Corinthians to "flee" sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:18), emphasizing a voluntary and decisive action against evil. This is moral flight: not panic, but prudence.

5. To escape the authority or control of someone: James states that if you resist the devil, "he will flee from you" (James 4:7). Here, the one fleeing is the devil himself, repelled by the believer's resistance.
G5343.origine: The Greek verb φεύγω comes from an ancient root expressing the idea of rapid movement and separation. In ancient Hebrew, the terms נוּס (nûs, "to flee") and בָּרַח (bâraḥ, "to escape") were primarily used, which cover the same meaning as the Greek: it is always the action of escaping danger by putting distance. The word belongs to a family of compound words in Greek (ἀποφεύγω, διαφεύγω, ἐκφεύγω) that nuance this idea of flight according to direction or intensity.
G5343.emploi: The verb "to flee" appears about 30 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke), in Acts, and in the pastoral epistles. It is first used literally: Joseph flees to Egypt (Matthew 2:13), the demon-possessed flee when they encounter Jesus (Mark 5:14), the disciples flee at His arrest (Mark 14:50). From Paul's teaching onward, the verb takes on a moral dimension: believers must flee idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:14), sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:18), and pursue righteousness (1 Timothy 6:11). In Revelation, it expresses cosmic chaos (the mountains flee before the throne of God, Revelation 16:20) or the defeat of evil. The meaning thus shifts from physical movement to spiritual and moral action: to flee from evil is to turn towards God.
G5343.portee: This word reminds Christians that faith is not passive: it requires deliberate action. To flee from evil is not just to passively avoid sin; it is to actively push it away, just as one would flee from danger. The image of flight, in Paul, invites vigilant prudence in the face of temptation. At the same time, the examples of flight in the Gospels show that God Himself guides those who need to escape peril—Joseph does not have to invent his own protection: he obeys divine orders. To flee, therefore, is also to trust in God.

sens: Roman governor of Judea in the 1st century
G5344.detail: Felix is a Roman procurator (governor) who administered Judea during the ministry of the apostle Paul. It is before him that Paul is brought in captivity to Caesarea, accused by the Jews. Felix hears Paul discourse on faith in Christ and on moral issues (justice, temperance, future judgment), but he refuses to go further and keeps him in custody, hoping to receive a bribe from him (Acts 24:24-26).
G5344.origine: The name Felix means "happy" or "fortunate" in Latin. It is an authentic Roman name, borne by several governors and important figures of the Empire. This Felix was the brother of the powerful freedman Pallas, which explained his political influence.
G5344.emploi: Felix appears in Acts during Paul's trial in Caesarea. He is mentioned 8 times as the governor to whom Paul is brought by the tribune Lysias for his protection (Acts 23:24, 26). Felix brings Paul to trial (Acts 24:22) and questions him with his wife Drusilla about the Christian faith (Acts 24:24-25). However, frightened by Paul's words about the coming judgment, he adjourns the case and leaves it pending, keeping Paul in prison perhaps awaiting a bribe. Felix is ultimately removed from office and replaced by Festus (Acts 24:27, 25:14).
G5344.portee: The portrait of Felix in Acts illustrates the weight of the Christian message on a conscience: even a powerful governor can be troubled by the truth of the Gospel. However, it also shows how fear and personal interests can hinder obedience to God. It is a lesson on the danger of indefinitely "postponing" a decision for Christ.

sens: Information, news, rumor that spreads
Reputation, renown that spreads among people
G5345.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to information or news that circulates from mouth to mouth, like a noise that gets out. In Matthew 9:26, after the resurrection of the synagogue leader's daughter, "the noise spread throughout the region": it is the news of this extraordinary miracle that reaches the entire country.
2. It can also refer to the reputation or fame that attaches to a person or event. In Luke 4:14, "the fame" of Jesus "spread throughout the surrounding country" after his ministry in Galilee: it is less a simple news item than a favorable estimation, a growing reputation.
G5345.origine: The word comes from the verb phêmi (φημί), which means "to say" or "to speak." Phêmē thus literally designates what is "said" or "spoken," hence the idea of a word that is transmitted and spreads. It is a common language word for any oral communication that circulates: a piece of news, a saying, a rumor, a reputation established by common speech.
G5345.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, always in a context where news or reputation spreads quickly. In Matthew 9:26, it refers to the miraculous news that arises after a remarkable event. In Luke 4:14, it designates the good reputation that accompanies the authority and power of Jesus' ministry. Both uses emphasize movement: the noise or fame "spreads" (or "has gone"), showing how the word acts as a force that gains ground and touches more and more people.
G5345.portee: This word reminds the reader of the power of word and testimony in the public life of Jesus. Miracles do not remain hidden: they create a fame, a reputation, a ripple effect. It is an encouragement to understand that our own faith and acts of obedience produce effects that extend beyond what we see, by the grace of God.

sens: to express in words, to pronounce words
to report someone else's words, to quote
to intervene in a conversation, to respond
to state a truth or assertion
to command, to order
G5346.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to emit words, to make one's voice heard. Jesus "said" to the one who tempted him: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God" (Matthew 4:7) — it is the simple act of speaking.
2. Very often, this verb introduces the direct speech of another person, faithfully reporting their words. Peter "said" to the crowd: "Repent" (Acts 2:38); it is the classic formula for quoting someone.
3. In a dialogue, "to say" can mean to intervene to respond or continue the conversation. Simon "answered" the Master: "Master, speak" (Luke 7:40) — here the verb marks the taking of the floor in an exchange.
4. Often the verb carries an assertion or declaration: Jesus "said" to the master: "Well done, good and faithful servant" (Matthew 25:23) — it is not just speaking, it is affirming and judging.
5. Sometimes "to say" expresses a command or instruction: Agrippa "said" to Paul: "You are permitted to speak for your defense" (Acts 26:1) — the authorization given by the word.
G5346.origine: The verb φημί comes from an ancient root meaning "to show, to make visible"; to say was originally to make heard and manifest one's thought. In Hebrew, this verb primarily translates נָאַם (nāʿam), which means "to proclaim, to affirm" with the idea of a solemn word, and also אָמַר (ʾāmar), the ordinary verb for "to say." This etymology suggests that saying is never a neutral act: it is always to make manifest, to assert something.
G5346.emploi: This verb appears about 66 times in the New Testament. It is extremely frequent in the four Gospels and in Acts, where it constantly serves to introduce the words of Jesus, the disciples, or other characters. Some uses employ it impersonally or formulaically: "it is said" (φησί), as in 1 Corinthians 6:16 where Paul quotes Scripture. The usage varies slightly: sometimes the verb simply means to speak (Matthew 4:7), sometimes it emphasizes the assertion or authority (Matthew 25:23), and sometimes it introduces a formal response in a trial or interrogation (Acts 26:1). The verb often combines with other speech formulas, enriching the narrative style.
G5346.portee: For the reader, this ordinary yet dense verb shows us that every word in the Bible — that of Jesus, that of the prophets, that of the disciples — is not a simple statement: it is an affirmation, a manifestation of thought and authority. When Jesus "says," it is never empty; when the disciples "say," it is that they are making a pronouncement. This invites us to listen not only to the words but to the weight of the biblical word.

sens: Roman procurator of Judea
Successor of Felix as head of the province
Judge of Paul on appeal before Caesar
G5347.detail: Festus is a Roman official appointed as procurator (governor) of Judea. He succeeded Felix around 60 AD (Acts 24:27). His main role in the Acts narrative is to judge the apostle Paul, who is imprisoned in Caesarea. When Paul appeals to Caesar to escape the accusations from the Jews, Festus accepts this request and declares: "You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go" (Acts 25:12). Festus is portrayed as a pragmatic administrator, seeking to manage a complicated judicial case in a climate of religious tensions. During the solemn hearing before King Agrippa II, he will accuse Paul of being out of his mind, not understanding the Christian faith (Acts 26:24).
G5347.origine: Festus is a Roman cognomen (family name), whose Latin form is Porcius Festus. The first name Porcius and the cognomen Festus are attested in Roman sources. In Greek, it is transliterated Φῆστος (Phēstos) in the text of the New Testament.
G5347.emploi: Festus appears thirteen times in Acts, solely in the account of Paul's trial (chapters 24 to 26). He is first presented as the successor of Felix (Acts 24:27). Then, he receives the accusations from the Jews against Paul, but he recognizes that the matter falls under the jurisdiction of Paul and King Agrippa (Acts 25:9-14). When Paul invokes the right to appeal to the Roman emperor, Festus validates this appeal (Acts 25:12). Finally, he presides over the public hearing where Paul addresses King Agrippa and the assembly, and it is there that he calls Paul mad, refusing to grasp the foundation of his testimony about the resurrection.
G5347.portee: Festus embodies the Roman political power of that time, just and legal in appearance, but unable to discern or receive the truth of the Gospel. His unbelief shows that earthly power and authority remain closed to the Christian message. However, Festus's presence in the narrative highlights how God uses Roman institutions for Paul to publicly testify, in accordance with the divine plan.

sens: To go before someone, arrive before them
To arrive at a place, reach
To achieve a goal or result
To occur, happen
G5348.detail:
1. To go before someone means to precede or arrive before them. It is the idea of passing ahead of another in a race or sequence: in 1 Thessalonians 4:15, Paul speaks of the living believers who will not precede those who have died — that is, they will not meet the Lord before the resurrected dead.
2. To arrive at a place or reach a destination: the kingdom of God has come to you (Matthew 12:28, Luke 11:20), meaning it has reached your location. Paul and his companions arrived at the Corinthians with the Gospel (2 Corinthians 10:14).
3. To achieve a goal, state, or result: Israel did not attain the law of righteousness that it sought (Romans 9:31), meaning it did not succeed in obtaining it. Believers have reached a certain point of spiritual progress (Philippians 3:16).
4. To occur or happen to a point: wrath has come upon the Jews who rejected the Gospel (1 Thessalonians 2:16), culminating in their sins — the idea of an accumulation that reaches its end.
G5348.origine: The verb φθάνω expresses the fundamental idea of arriving or coming to a place, often with the nuance of going before or preceding. In classical Greek, it originally meant "to come before, to anticipate." In later texts and the spoken Greek of the New Testament, the meaning expanded to simply "to arrive, to reach." The root evokes movement toward a point, like something that reaches its destination.
G5348.emploi: The verb φθάνω appears 7 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. It carries two main meanings: 1) to go before or precede (1 Thessalonians 4:15); 2) to arrive, reach a place or goal (Matthew 12:28, Luke 11:20, Romans 9:31, 2 Corinthians 10:14, Philippians 3:16, 1 Thessalonians 2:16). In the accounts of Jesus, the verb describes the arrival of the kingdom of God to the listeners. In Paul, it designates both the physical arrival of the apostle at the churches and the attainment of a spiritual goal or state.
G5348.portee: This verb reminds us that the kingdom of God truly comes to people, that the Gospel spreads concretely and changes lives. For Paul, it invites the believer to progress in their walk with Christ and not to lag behind. The word also emphasizes the reality of divine providence: what God intends to accomplish always ends up reaching us.

sens: That decomposes, rots, loses its qualities over time
That is mortal, subject to death and destruction
That can be seduced, capable of sinning and doing evil
That has no lasting value, not worthy of an eternal price
G5349.detail:
1. A corruptible being is one whose body degrades and disappears: this is the case for man, for his perishable flesh (1 Peter 1:23). This corruption is not a moral fate, but a physical reality of our mortal condition.
2. The word also designates what is mortal, destined to disappear: a winner's crown at the Olympic games may be made of laurel that withers, while the Christian runs for a crown that does not fade (1 Corinthians 9:25).
3. Corruptible opposes incorruptible when it comes to the very nature: our mortal body must put on immortality at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53-54), passing from corruption to incorruptibility.
4. By extension, corruptible are material riches — silver and gold — that cannot redeem the soul and cannot be relied upon for eternal salvation (1 Peter 1:18).
G5349.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb meaning "to destroy, to spoil." It forms a pair with its opposite "incorruptible": while man and all that is created are corruptible, God alone is incorruptible in His divine nature. This distinction between the corruptible and the incorruptible is fundamental in biblical thought to oppose the temporal to the eternal.
G5349.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the first epistle of Peter. Paul uses it to contrast mortal human nature with the incorruptible God (Romans 1:23), and to explain the necessary transformation of the body at the resurrection: what is corruptible must put on incorruptibility (1 Corinthians 15:53-54). He also uses it to belittle earthly rewards compared to the eternal crown (1 Corinthians 9:25). Peter uses it to emphasize that neither silver nor gold — corruptible things — can redeem us, unlike the living word of God that has regenerated us (1 Peter 1:18, 1:23). The word consistently carries a dimension of opposition: corruptible versus incorruptible, temporal versus eternal.
G5349.portee: This word reminds the Christian that everything purely material and earthly — our riches, our honors, our current body — is marked by finitude and death. It invites us not to place our trust in these things that disappear, but in what is eternal: the word of God and the new life it gives. The Christian hope lies in the fact that, through the resurrection, we who are currently corruptible and mortal will be transformed to put on incorruptibility and immortality.

sens: to produce a sound, a voice
to express oneself orally
to take the floor to say something
G5350.detail:
1. The basic meaning is to emit a sound or a voice: this is what living beings do when they communicate through speech. In 2 Peter 2:16, the donkey "stopped the madness of the prophet" by making "a voice of a man" heard — it produced a human sound, which restrained him.
2. The verb means to express oneself orally, to say something with words. In Acts 4:18, the authorities forbade the apostles to "speak" in the name of Jesus: to forbid speaking is to forbid witnessing, announcing.
3. In some contexts, the verb pertains to the very content of what is said: in 2 Peter 2:18, some "speak" of arrogant and excessive words ("profess"), which shows that the verb encompasses what is said.
G5350.origine: The word φθέγγομαι is an ancient Greek verb that literally means "to give a cry" or "to emit a sound." It evokes the primitive image of a creature producing a sound from its throat. It often translates the Hebrew עָנָה (ànâ, to answer, to speak) and נָבַע (nâbaʻ, to gush forth, to flow — for the word that escapes). It is a rather rare and solemn verb, emphasizing the act of producing a voice rather than the detailed content of the speech.
G5350.emploi: The verb φθέγγομαι appears only three times in the New Testament, always in serious and significant contexts. In Acts 4:18, it describes the prohibition placed on the apostles to "speak" in the name of Jesus — an act of apostolic censorship. In 2 Peter 2:16, it designates the human voice that the donkey of the prophet uttered to rebuke him — a miracle of divine communication. In 2 Peter 2:18, it signifies the inflated words that false teachers utter. The verb seems preferred when speech carries particular weight: an official command, a miraculous event, a condemnable word.
G5350.portee: This verb reminds the reader that a word is never insignificant: it is an act, a voice that comes from the mouth and carries weight. For the apostles, the prohibition to "speak" strikes at their very mission; for the false teachers, their inflated words condemn them. The Christian discovers here that every word counts — the one we risk losing in silence, the one that testifies against injustice, and the one we utter in vain.

sens: Completely destroy something physically
Alter, spoil the quality or integrity of something
Morally deprave, lead away from good
Damage, ruin a relationship or trust
G5351.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of physical destruction: to destroy, to annihilate. In 1 Corinthians 3:17, Paul uses it literally: "If anyone destroys the temple of God" (the building of worship), "God will destroy him."
2. But the word also means to alter or corrupt the nature of something, without necessarily completely destroying it. In 1 Corinthians 15:33, "bad company corrupts good morals": good behaviors are gradually spoiled, degraded by bad influences.
3. It applies to inner moral corruption: in Ephesians 4:22, "the old man who is corrupted by deceitful desires" shows how deceitful desires rot the soul from within, leading it away from God.
4. The verb also refers to the destruction of integrity or trust: in 2 Corinthians 7:2, Paul says, "we have wronged no one," meaning he did not exploit or destroy the trust relationship with the Corinthians.
G5351.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root evoking the action of spoiling, altering, or breaking. It appears in the New Testament to translate the ancient Hebrew "šāḥat" (to destroy, to corrupt), commonly used in the Old Testament to speak of moral corruption or destruction. The word family includes compounds like "diaphtheirō" (to completely corrupt) and "kataphtheirō" (to totally destroy). This root always expresses the idea of a transition from a good state to a bad state.
G5351.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul’s writings and in the epistles. In 1 Corinthians 3:17 and 15:33, it denotes concrete or moral destruction: that of the temple or that of morals. In 2 Corinthians, it takes on the shade of personal grievance: not corrupting the trust of the faithful is a proof of apostolic integrity. In Ephesians 4:22, it speaks of the inner degradation of the heart through sin. In 2 Peter 2:12 and Jude 10, it describes how false teachers will be destroyed themselves, as they destroy themselves. Everywhere, the verb carries the idea of serious, irreversible, and fatal deterioration.
G5351.portee: This word reminds Christians that sin is a force of destruction — not only of external things but of the soul itself. It invites us to keep our moral integrity and that of the community pure, as bad influences silently work to corrupt from within. It is also a warning: those who live in sin destroy themselves, and God will not leave unpunished those who destroy His people or His Church.

sens: Belonging to the season of autumn
Sterile, unproductive at the time when it should bear fruit
G5352.detail:
1. The word simply designates what belongs to autumn, the season at the end of the year. Jude speaks of "autumn trees" to paint a picture of desolation.
2. But Jude's text adds a nuance: these autumn trees are "without fruit." In autumn, one would expect trees to have borne their fruit, yet these trees remain barren — an image of false teachers who produce no spiritual good despite their claims to teach. They are "twice dead, uprooted": dead by their sterile nature, and destined to be pulled up.
G5352.origine: The Greek word comes from "phthinopōron" which literally means "the season of decline" (root: phthinein, to decline, and pōron, relating to supply). It is a poetic composition that depicts autumn as the time when nature declines and is emptied of its fruits. The biblical image of missing fruit in autumn underscores the anomaly: a tree must produce; if it does not, it is either dead or cursed.
G5352.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:12. Jude uses it in a denunciation of the heretics who have infiltrated the Church. These false teachers are compared to fruitless trees in autumn: they promise spiritual nourishment and teaching but deliver nothing. The image is particularly biting: not only do they not produce, but they harm, shamelessly eating at the communion meals (the agapes) while leaving the community spiritually hungry.
G5352.portee: This image shows us that true faith must bear fruit. A fruitless tree has no reason to exist; likewise, a teacher or doctor who does not produce justice, love, and holiness is spiritually dead. It invites us to examine our own lives: are we bearing fruit, or are we like these autumn trees, empty of any lasting work?

sens: A noise, a sound vibration perceptible to the ear
Specifically, a voice or a cry
A musical note or sound emitted by an instrument
G5353.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a noise or sound in the physical sense: what the ear hears when something vibrates or produces an audible vibration. In Romans 10:18, Paul quotes Psalm 19, saying that "the voice" (the sound) of creation extends throughout the earth — it is the echo or noise of divine order resonating everywhere.
2. It specifically refers to a human voice, a cry, or a word: the sound manifestation of the person speaking. This is also what is heard in Romans 10:18: the voice of creatures testifying to God.
3. It can also designate a precise note or distinct musical sound: in 1 Corinthians 14:7, Paul speaks of "distinct sounds" from a flute or a harp — clear and differentiable notes, without which one could not recognize the melody played. The idea is one of clear articulation, a sound expression that can truly be identified.
G5353.origine: The word comes from the verb φθέγγομαι (phtheggomai), which means "to speak, to pronounce, to emit a sound." The root evokes vocal emission, the act of making one's voice heard. In Greek, this family of words is always related to the production of an audible sound, whether human or not. The central idea is that of a sound vibration that propagates and can be perceived.
G5353.emploi: The word appears only twice in Greek in the New Testament. In Romans 10:18, quoted from Psalm 19, it designates the "voice" (the audible testimony) of creation proclaiming God. In 1 Corinthians 14:7, Paul uses it to describe the sounds of musical instruments, particularly the importance of producing "distinct notes" (a possible translation of the same word): without this sound clarity, one could not understand the melody. In both cases, the word emphasizes the audible, recognizable, and meaningful nature of sound.
G5353.portee: This word reminds us that communication — whether divine (like the testimony of creation) or human (like speech during a gathering) — relies on clarity of expression. In the Church, the sound must be distinct for the message to be understood; in creation, the sound of the world testifies to its Creator. It is an invitation to make our words clear and our actions meaningful.

sens: to feel resentment at the success or advantage of others
to desire what someone else possesses with bitterness
to be consumed by jealousy because of another's qualities or possessions
G5354.detail:
1. To envy is to feel an inner bitterness when seeing someone else succeed, possess, or be recognized. Envy is the painful resentment faced with the good of others — not the innocent desire to also possess something, but the jealous rage that another possesses it. In Galatians 5:26, Paul warns believers: do not provoke one another by seeking vain glory and envying one another, for this jealousy tears apart the body of Christ and kills unity.
2. Envy is primarily a personal feeling that boils silently, but it quickly drives the one who feels it to show hostility or malice towards the one they envy. This is why Paul lists it among the works of the flesh: it ruins brotherly relationships and makes communal life in the Christian community impossible.
G5354.origine: The verb φθονέω comes from the noun φθόνος (phthónos), which denotes envy, jealousy, malice. This root expresses the feeling of resentment and covetousness that arises when one compares their lot to that of another. The Greek verb conveys the idea of being eaten away by jealousy, of being consumed by envy. It is a classical Greek word, rarely used in the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, where it barely appears in Tobit.
G5354.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 5:26. Paul uses it in his warning to the Galatian churches that threaten to divide themselves through pride and rivalry. Envy is presented there not as a simple feeling of admiration, but as a destructive passion that pits believers against one another. The context shows that Paul combats the effects of the flesh — the rivalries of prestige and jealousy — that divert Christians from living according to the Spirit. This word is among the works of the flesh that prevent the inheritance of the kingdom.
G5354.portee: Envy is a spiritual poison that the Christian must recognize and reject. By naming it, Paul helps believers identify what destroys the unity of the Church: not only gross covetousness but also this subtle jealousy that arises when one compares themselves to a brother or sister. Learning not to envy is choosing to rejoice in the good of others and to find one's dignity in Christ alone, not in rivalry.

sens: Feeling of displeasure and malice towards the goods or qualities of others
Malice that drives one to harm or thwart someone
Jealous rivalry in proclaiming the faith
Evil passion accompanying pride and quarrels
G5355.detail:
1. Envy is primarily this painful feeling that arises from seeing the good in others — their wealth, success, prestige, or gifts. It is a jealousy that denies the other their place, as when the chief priests deliver Jesus out of envy for his success with the crowd (Matthew 27:18).
2. This envy becomes malicious: it does not merely feel displeasure, it drives one to contrary action, to hinder or harm the one they envy. It is linked to quarrels, slander, and bad suspicions (1 Timothy 6:4).
3. In preaching, envy creates unhealthy rivalry: one proclaims Christ not out of love but out of envy, eager to eclipse other preachers (Philippians 1:15).
4. Finally, envy belongs to the biblical catalog of destructive passions, alongside pride, disputes, drunkenness (Galatians 5:21, Romans 1:29), as a characteristic trait of humanity estranged from God.
G5355.origine: The Greek word « phthonos » literally expresses the evil eye, the resentment of seeing another enjoy a good. In ancient Greek, it is a malady of the soul that gnaws at the one who feels it. The Greek versions of the Old Testament used it to translate contexts of malicious jealousy. It is a specifically human passion, born from the refusal to accept the order established by God.
G5355.emploi: Envy appears nine times in the New Testament, concentrated in the epistles and in the Passion narrative. In Matthew and Mark, it explains why the religious authorities delivered Jesus: they envy his influence. In Paul's lists of vices (Romans 1:29, Galatians 5:21, 1 Timothy 6:4, Titus 3:3), envy is alongside pride, quarrels, and slander — it never manifests alone, but always among other sins of division and hostility. In Philippians 1:15 and 1 Timothy 6:4, it generates disputes and rivalry even in holy matters. James 4:5 attributes to it a desire so violent that it embraces a person's entire spirit. It is always an evil to be rejected.
G5355.portee: Envy is exposed as a poison that destroys both the one who harbors it and those who fall victim to it. Recognizing envy within oneself — this resentment towards the gifts or success of a brother — is to identify a root of discord capable of dividing the church and corrupting the testimony. Matthew and Mark remind us that envy led to the death of Christ: it is serious. But Philippians 1:15 also shows that the truth of Christ triumphs even over the envy of those who preach it — a lesson of consolation for anyone oppressed by the jealousy of others.

sens: Physical destruction or decomposition of a thing
Mortal and perishable character of a body or creature
Moral ruin, vice, or depravity
That which is subject to destruction and death
G5356.detail:
1. Corruption is primarily physical destruction, the decomposition of a thing. When the Segond speaks of a "corruptible" body, it refers to a body that can rot, degrade, or disappear (1 Corinthians 15:42).
2. More broadly, it denotes everything that is mortal and destined to perish — everything that lacks eternal life. Creation itself, according to Paul, is "subject to the bondage of corruption" (Romans 8:21): it ages, wears out, and does not have life in itself.
3. Corruption can also be moral: it is the inner ruin of a person, the vice that spoils them from within. Peter denounces those who wallow "in corruption" (2 Peter 2:12), that is, in the passions that degrade and destroy them.
4. By extension, corruption simply designates anything that is subject to destruction — opposed to eternal life (Galatians 6:8): "he who sows to his flesh will reap corruption."
G5356.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb meaning "to destroy, spoil, corrupt." The image is that of something rotting, disintegrating, losing its integrity. In Hebrew and Aramaic, there were similar words to express destruction, ruin, annihilation — these terms that the Greek Church chose to render as corruption. It is a word that unites the physical image (a body decomposing) and the moral image (a soul that vice destroys).
G5356.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and Peter. In Paul, it describes the mortal condition of all creation (Romans 8:21) and of the human body that must be resurrected (1 Corinthians 15:42, 50) — corruption is what resurrection will conquer. He also contrasts corruption and eternal life: he who sows to the flesh reaps corruption, but he who sows to the Spirit reaps eternal life (Galatians 6:8). In Peter, the word also carries a moral charge: it designates the disorder of desires, the covetousness that destroys the soul (2 Peter 1:4, 2:12, 2:19). It is presented as the enemy to flee, the evil to be avoided by remaining attached to the divine nature.
G5356.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals a terrible yet comforting reality. Terrible: everything that is not eternal is destined to rot, to disappear — our mortal body, the pleasures of the world, even human precepts. Comforting: this corruption does not have the final word. God promises those who sow to the Spirit not corruption, but eternal life (Galatians 6:8); he will send an incorruptible resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:42). Fleeing corruption is choosing to cling to what lasts, to what cannot die.

sens: Shallow, wide, and open container intended for pouring liquids
In a figurative sense, what is poured or spilled, particularly the contents poured (anger, judgment)
Symbol of fate, what is reserved for us
G5357.detail:
1. A cup is a shallow, wide, and open bowl — the opposite of a narrow vase. The Greeks used them for libations, that is, to ritually pour wine or perfumes in honor of a deity. John sees in a vision the twenty-four elders around the throne of God, each holding a golden cup filled with perfumes, which represent the prayers of the saints (Revelation 5:8).
2. In Revelation, the cup primarily symbolizes what is poured — particularly the anger and judgment of God. The seven angels each receive a cup of divine wrath and will pour it out on the earth: when the first pours his cup, plagues appear; when the second pours it on the sea, it becomes blood and every living being dies (Revelation 16:1-3). Thus, the cup becomes the instrument of divine judgment.
3. Symbolically, the cup also represents fate or destiny — what befalls us, what awaits us. It is the biblical image of the chalice that one must drink: accepting what God allows or decides for us.
G5357.origine: The Greek word phialē originally designates a concrete object: a shallow cup used for libations. In biblical Hebrew and Aramaic, the word mizraq (מִזְרָק) is found, which has the same meaning of a cultic object for pouring. The translation of the Hebrew word by phialē in the Greek Bible (the Septuagint) shows that both cultures shared this ritual practice. The word evokes the very action of pouring, hence its figurative use to designate what is poured.
G5357.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, exclusively in Revelation. It is never used in the Gospels or in the epistles. In Revelation, it first refers to the golden cups full of perfumes that the elders hold before the throne (5:8), an image of prayer rising to God. Then, and especially, it designates the seven cups of divine wrath that the angels successively pour out on the earth, the sea, the rivers, and the sun (16:1-17). Finally, an angel uses the word to announce to John the judgment of Babylon, the great prostitute (17:1). The word oscillates between the material object and what it contains or represents: the cup itself and the judgment it pours out.
G5357.portee: Understanding the cup of Revelation helps the reader grasp that God's judgment is not abstract: it is something poured out, deployed, real. It also reminds us that in the liturgy of heaven, the prayers of the saints rise to the throne of God and are precious — they have weight and efficacy. For the Christian, this word invites reflection on what we 'drink' or accept from the hand of God, and on the certainty that His judgment, though fearsome, is just and ultimately pacified by the grace of Christ.

sens: one who loves what is good, just, and virtuous
one who cherishes good works and moral virtues
G5358.detail:
1. This word designates someone who sincerely and actively loves what is good and virtuous. It is not the love of a person, but of the just and moral values themselves. In Titus 1:8, Paul describes the ideal bishop as 'lover of good,' showing that a church leader must have a deep attachment to justice and righteousness.

2. Beyond a simple preference, it describes someone who actively seeks good and draws near to it — a lover of good deeds and virtues. It is the disposition of the heart that loves to do what pleases God and builds up others.
G5358.origine: The word is composed of φίλος (friend, one who loves) and ἀγαθός (good, virtuous). This combination expresses love or attachment to a moral quality. It is a common word in Greek philosophy to describe the virtuous man — someone who loves good as a friend loves his companion.
G5358.emploi: Paul uses this word only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:8, to enumerate the qualities of the bishop. It appears in his list of required virtues: hospitable, lover of good, moderate, just, holy, self-controlled. This passage shows that one who leads the church must be marked not only by the absence of vice but by an active love for good and justice. It is a quality of mature moral life.
G5358.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that good is not a burdensome obligation, but something to love. A spiritual leader, and indeed every believer, must cultivate a genuine affection for what pleases God — not out of legal obligation, but from a heart's attraction to justice and virtue. It is a call to do good with joy and passion.

sens: Ancient city of Lydia, in Asia Minor (modern Turkey)
Local church mentioned in Revelation
G5359.detail:
1. Philadelphia is an ancient city located in Lydia, a region of Asia Minor. Its Greek name literally means 'brotherly love' (from 'philos', friend, and 'adelphos', brother), but it is best known as one of the seven cities where Christian churches existed during John's time.
2. In Revelation, the church of Philadelphia receives a special message from the risen Christ, who presents Himself as 'the one who has the key of David, who opens, and no one will shut' (Revelation 3:7). It is one of the seven churches to which John must send his book (Revelation 1:11).
G5359.origine: The name Philadelphia comes from the Greek 'philos' (friend, to love) and 'adelphos' (brother), literally meaning 'brotherly love' or 'fraternal affection'. The city was founded in the 2nd century BC by Attalus II of Pergamum, who named it in honor of his love for his brother. This name reflects the Hellenistic ideal of fraternal friendship, a notion that the New Testament will take up under the term 'philadelphia' to designate the love that Christians should have for one another.
G5359.emploi: Philadelphia is one of the seven churches of Asia mentioned in Revelation. It appears twice: in the list of the seven churches that John must warn (Revelation 1:11), and in the specific message that the risen Christ addresses to His church (Revelation 3:7-13). Unlike some other churches mentioned, Philadelphia receives a message without reproach, praised for its faithfulness despite its apparent weakness. The city itself has persisted into modern times under another name.
G5359.portee: The church of Philadelphia embodies discreet and patient faithfulness. The message of Christ to this church reminds us that God rewards not visible human power, but perseverance in obedience and brotherly love — a theme consistent with the very meaning of the city's name. For the Christian reader, Philadelphia symbolizes a church that keeps the word of God and does not deny His name, despite trials.

sens: Natural affection between blood brothers
Affection among members of the same community, as among brothers
Mutual and sincere love among the children of God
G5360.detail:
1. In the most literal sense, it is the affection that brothers naturally feel for one another due to their blood relationship. It is familial sentiment, the warm bond between those who share the same family.

2. The Bible transposes this natural tenderness to the life of the Church: it designates the mutual affection that Christians should have for one another, as if they were brothers and sisters. In 1 Thessalonians 4:9, Paul commends these Christians who have already learned from God to show this brotherly love.

3. This brotherly love is not a vague sympathy, but a sincere and persevering dedication. In 1 Peter 1:22, it is a "sincere" love that urges to "love one another earnestly, from the heart." In Hebrews 13:1, we are asked to "persevere" in this love, showing that it must be cultivated constantly.
G5360.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: φίλος (friend, beloved) and ἀδελφός (brother). Literally, it means the love of a brother. This evocative composition shows how the Greek language constructs the word by bringing together love and brotherhood. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the idea is found in words speaking of friendship or affection between brothers, but the Greek of the New Testament forges this specific term to express relational warmth within the Christian community.
G5360.emploi: This word appears five times in the New Testament, always in relation to the apostolic letters addressed to the churches. Paul uses it to encourage the Thessalonians, who are already practicing this virtue: he does not ask them to start, but to persevere in what they have received. The letter to the Hebrews makes it a clear and unavoidable requirement. Peter's epistles place it in the broader context of spiritual growth: in 2 Peter 1:7, brotherly love is presented as a necessary step on the path that leads to universal charity (the love of all men). Everywhere, this love is never abstract: it materializes in gestures, mutual kindness, and sincerity of heart.
G5360.portee: Brotherly love reminds the believer that the Church is not just an organization or an institution, but a true family. It is an antidote to indifference and selfishness: being a Christian means agreeing to treat one another with the tenderness and dedication natural to brothers. This biblical requirement invites each disciple to concretely examine the quality of their relationships within the assembly: am I eager in kindness towards my brothers and sisters? Is my love for them sincere and sustained, or superficial and inconsistent?

sens: Feeling of affection and goodwill between brothers
Deep friendship characterized by intimacy and loyalty
Love that Christians should have for one another, as among members of the same family
G5361.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the natural love between blood brothers — this deep familial bond that unites the children of the same family. It is a spontaneous love, based on the blood relationship and the intimacy shared from childhood.

2. In a broader sense, it designates any exceptional friendship marked by brotherhood and mutual trust, as expressed by ancient Greek writers: a loyalty without calculation, a manly tenderness.

3. In the New Testament, this word applies to the love that Christians should cultivate for one another. In 1 Peter 3:8, the apostle exhorts believers to be "full of brotherly love" — that is, to treat one another as brothers and sisters, beyond their carnal ties, because they together form the family of God. This love is not just a feeling, but a choice, an attitude of heart to maintain and cultivate.
G5361.origine: The word is composed of "philo-" (to love) and "adelphos" (brother). It expresses the idea of the love that binds brothers. The root "philo-" appears in other Greek words describing different forms of love (friendship, goodwill, tenderness). The Greek word often translates the Hebrew concept of brotherly love in the Old Testament, particularly in later traditions where community sentiment took on new importance.
G5361.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:8. Peter uses it to urge scattered believers to actively cultivate brotherly love as an essentially Christian virtue. Although rare in the New Testament, this term summarizes a central conviction: believers form a united family, and this mutual love is the cement of their communion. The context shows that it is a conscious and voluntary love, not a passive feeling, as it is placed on the same level as compassion and humility as attitudes of the heart to cultivate.
G5361.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize that their spiritual ties with other believers are as real and as close as carnal family ties. Brotherly love is not a vague feeling, but a concrete attachment, attentive to the needs of others and oriented towards the good of a brother or sister in Christ. It is a call to transcend divisions and differences to live in true communion of heart.

sens: Who loves her husband
Who is faithful and devoted to her spouse
G5362.detail: 1. This word designates a woman who loves her husband — not a fleeting feeling, but a solid affection and a lasting attachment. In Titus 2:4, Paul asks that older women teach the younger ones to "love their husbands": it is about cultivating tenderness and loyalty towards the husband, at the heart of a stable marital life. 2. The love mentioned here is also a form of dedication and self-giving. The woman who loves her husband supports him, respects him, and seeks his well-being — it is a commitment of the heart that underpins the unity of the couple.
G5362.origine: The word comes from the Greek root phílos (friend, one who loves) combined with andros (man, husband). It literally designates one who "loves the man" or more precisely who loves her husband. This compound was common in Greek epitaphs to honor the memory of virtuous and loving women.
G5362.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Titus 2:4. Paul exhorts Titus to teach young women to love their husbands (and their children), as part of Christian wisdom and orderly family life. It fits within a set of moral and spiritual qualities that Paul expects from Christian living.
G5362.portee: This term reminds us that marital love — sincere affection and dedication of the couple — is at the heart of Christian family life. Paul does not present it as an arbitrary obligation, but as a virtue to cultivate and learn, essential for the stability and joy of the home. It is an invitation to see love for the husband as a spiritual and human treasure to maintain.

sens: An attitude of one who seeks the good of others, a form of kindness and compassion
Goodness that is shown towards strangers or the unfortunate
Expression of God's love for humanity
G5363.detail:
1. Benevolence is the feeling that drives someone to wish well for others, to act with kindness and compassion. It is an active goodness that is realized in concrete gestures: in Acts 28:2, the inhabitants of Malta show an "unusual benevolence" to the shipwrecked by welcoming them and lighting a fire to warm them.
2. It is also the humanity that one shows towards strangers, victims of misfortune, those in need. The warm welcome of the Maltese towards Paul and his companions illustrates this goodness that extends even to strangers.
3. It can refer to God's benevolent love for humanity: in Titus 3:4, God's "goodness" and His "love for mankind" (His benevolence towards humanity) are manifested when He saves us. It is a divine tenderness that goes beyond mere duty and expresses God's affection for His creation.
G5363.origine: The word comes from the Greek φιλέω (philéô, to love) and ἄνθρωπος (anthrôpos, man): it literally means "love for mankind." It is a humanitarian virtue, a feeling that unites love and responsibility towards others. The word also appears in the Greek text of the Old Testament, notably in the Maccabees, to describe the goodness of kings towards their subjects.
G5363.emploi: The word is rare in the New Testament: it is found only twice. In Acts 28:2, it describes an admirable quality of the Maltese who generously welcome Paul and his companions in distress. In Titus 3:4, Paul uses it to speak of the goodness and love that God shows towards humanity in salvation. In both cases, it is a benevolence that translates into concrete and generous acts: hospitality among the Maltese, salvation from God.
G5363.portee: This benevolence invites us to consider how we treat strangers, the unfortunate, those in need. The testimony of the Maltese shows that such goodness is remarkable and impressive. But above all, in Titus 3:4, we see that all human benevolence comes from God's primary goodness towards us: it is because God loved us and saved us that we can in turn show this same tenderness towards others.

sens: In a humane and benevolent manner
With kindness and consideration for others
G5364.detail:
1. In a humane and benevolent manner: the word denotes an attitude of respect and kindness towards others, treating each person with humanity. In Acts 27:3, the centurion Julius treats Paul "with benevolence" by allowing him to go to friends for care — a gesture of human consideration towards a prisoner.
2. With kindness and consideration for others: it is acting not out of obligation, but from a natural concern for the well-being of others. This benevolence reflects a form of respect that honors the dignity of the person.
G5364.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "philo" (love) and "anthropos" (human, man). Together, they form an adverb meaning literally "in a friend of humanity." It is a classical Greek virtue, the love of humankind — not a personal friendship, but a general disposition of kindness towards all. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, this word appears rarely, highlighting its later use in the Greek biblical tradition.
G5364.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:3. It describes how the centurion Julius welcomes Paul during the journey to Rome — not as a mere prisoner, but as a man worthy of consideration. The context shows a Roman officer who, despite the burden of oversight, acts with humanity and benevolence. The usage underscores the contrast between the rigor of Roman justice and the possible human kindness it can contain.
G5364.portee: This word reminds Christians that benevolence is a universal virtue, recognized even outside of faith. A pagan centurion can embody this quality. For the believer, it is an invitation to treat everyone with respect and humanity, as Jesus teaches, seeing in each person someone worthy of consideration. This practical, simple, and concrete benevolence often speaks louder than words.

sens: Passionate attachment to money and wealth
Intense desire to possess and accumulate material goods
Thirst for gain that dominates the heart
G5365.detail:
1. The word literally denotes the love (philéo) directed towards money (argyros). It is a passion, an attachment of the heart to wealth, making money the primary object of one's desires and efforts. The classic example is 1 Timothy 6:10, where Paul calls the love of money "a root of all evils."
2. It is more than a mere passing desire: it is a dominant tendency to want to possess and accumulate material goods, a thirst for gain that grows without ever being satisfied.
3. This word depicts less the covetousness towards a particular good of another than the general orientation of the heart towards personal enrichment: it is to desire money for itself, making it the center of one's life.
G5365.origine: The word is composed of two parts: philéo (to love) and argyros (money, precious metal). The basic image is therefore love, the affection one usually has for a person, but here directed towards material wealth as if it were a personal good to cherish. This formation in "philo-" (friend of, lover of) is common in Greek to denote the inclinations of the heart.
G5365.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:10. Paul identifies the love of money not as a simple sin among others, but as "a root of all evils" — that is, as the soil from which many disorders arise: dishonesty, covetousness, abandonment of faith. This passage shows that for the apostle, it is a serious spiritual problem in the Church, affecting even those who have known Christ.
G5365.portee: This word calls the believer to examine their heart: has money become for them the object of a passionate love? Scripture does not condemn the possession of goods, but warns against the enslavement of the heart to wealth. Recognizing this love of money within oneself is the first step to being freed from it and placing one's affection where it should be: in God and in eternal things.

sens: One who loves money and desires it passionately
One who refuses to give or share due to attachment to wealth
G5366.detail:
1. The word primarily describes someone who is drawn to money with a guilty, almost pathological affection. It is a misplaced love: one loves money as one should love God or one's neighbor. The Pharisees in Luke 16:14, "greedy," listen to Jesus speak about wealth and serving God, but they mock Him because His message threatens their attachment to gold. It is the idolatry of wealth.
2. The word then denotes the habit of accumulating without giving, of clutching one's purse. In 2 Timothy 3:2, Paul lists the vices of the last days: "lovers of money," meaning men who sacrifice everything—love, generosity, even piety—to possess more. Greed is not merely a weakness: it is a sin that corrupts the entire heart.
G5366.origine: The Greek word is composed of two roots: "philo" (to love) and "argyros" (money). This composition clearly shows that it is a misdirected love, an affection turned toward a bad end. It is a word simply formed in Greek to mean "one who loves money"—just as one might say "one who loves horses" or "one who loves glory." The Hebrew Old Testament uses similar imagery to describe covetousness (for example, the Hebrew word translated as "greed"), but this specific Greek word appears only here in the New Testament.
G5366.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, and each usage sheds light on an aspect of the same vice. In Luke 16:14, Jesus has just told the parable of the dishonest manager and asserts that one cannot serve two masters—God and money. The Pharisees, "greedy," react with disdain: Jesus has touched an open wound. In 2 Timothy 3:2, Paul places greed among the major sins of the last days, alongside selfishness and pride: it is never a minor vice in the eyes of Scripture. The Greek word is translated sometimes as "greedy" (Luke), sometimes as "lover of money" (2 Timothy), but it is the same heart defect.
G5366.portee: For a Christian, this word is a serious warning and a call to self-examination. Greed is modern idolatry, the lie of the heart that whispers: "wealth will save me, wealth will fulfill me." Jesus invites us to ask: who or what truly binds me? To whom does my deep affection belong? The antidote to greed is not forced poverty, but trust in God and liberated generosity.

sens: one who loves oneself, who prefers oneself above all
one who seeks one's own advantage at the expense of others
one who is self-centered and indifferent to the needs of others
G5367.detail: 1. The word literally designates one who loves oneself—one might break it down to "lover of oneself." It is the attitude of one who places their own interest at the heart of all their decisions (2 Timothy 3:2). 2. In its moral sense, it is selfishness: the disposition to seek one's profit or pleasure without regard for others, especially in relationships where generosity and sharing should prevail. 3. It is also a form of spiritual blindness: the selfish person sees only themselves and their needs, which isolates them from others and cuts them off from God's grace.
G5367.origine: The Greek word combines "philo" (to love) and "autos" (oneself): it is literally the love of oneself. Among Greek philosophers, this trait was already recognized as a vice. In the Bible, it characterizes the state of the human heart left to itself, far from the love of God and neighbor.
G5367.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:2, where Paul describes the difficult times of the last days. He lists the vices that will mark society, and selfishness comes first: "men will be selfish." Paul thus emphasizes that self-love becomes the root of all the evils listed afterward: love of money, boastfulness, pride, blasphemy. It is the portrait of humanity closed off from God.
G5367.portee: For the believer, this word is a warning: selfishness, even when it hides under the guise of ambition or personal responsibility, is incompatible with the Christian faith. Jesus teaches to deny oneself and to love one's neighbor as oneself. Recognizing one's natural selfishness invites the Christian to ask God to transform their heart and free them from this prison of self.

sens: To feel affection and friendship for someone
To have a taste for, a preference for something
To kiss someone as a sign of affection or respect
G5368.detail:
1. To love someone is to feel for them a personal affection, a sincere friendship: a heartfelt sentiment that leads to tenderness and attachment. Jesus asks Peter: "Do you love me?" (John 21:16), expecting a response that expresses the disciple's personal affection, far beyond mere duty. The Father loves the Son with an intimate love (John 5:20).
2. To love a thing is to have a taste for it, to want to draw near to it. Hypocrites "love" to pray standing in the synagogues (Matthew 6:5): it is not that they adore prayer, but that they seek it for the vain glory it brings them. One can also love one's own life, but to the point of refusing to lose it for Christ (John 12:25).
3. To kiss someone is to express through this gesture one's affection, respect, or sometimes—like in the case of Judas—a false friendship (Matthew 26:48). The kiss was in the East a normal sign of welcome among friends.
G5368.origine: The word comes from the root φίλ- which expresses friendship, personal affection (it is found in "philosophy," the love of wisdom, or in the adjective φίλος, "friend"). In Hebrew, it primarily translates the verb אָהַב (to love) which describes affection, and sometimes נָשַׁק (to kiss). Greek distinguishes between φιλέω (to love with heartfelt sentiment) and ἀγαπάω (to love voluntarily and respectfully), although the two touch upon each other.
G5368.emploi: This verb appears about 21 times in the New Testament, notably in the Gospel of John and the epistles. John often uses it to describe Jesus' personal love for His disciples or God's love for humanity (John 5:20, 11:3, 16:27). Matthew and Mark use it to recount Judas' kiss (Matthew 26:48, Mark 14:44), where simulated friendship becomes betrayal. The verb is also used to express desire, preference: to love the first place (Matthew 23:6), to love to pray to be noticed (Matthew 6:5). Paul imbues it with a value of personal connection in prayer (1 Corinthians 16:22: "Let anyone who does not love the Lord be accursed"). Its meaning oscillates between intimate affection and simple preference depending on the context.
G5368.portee: This word reminds the believer that the love at the heart of the Gospel is personal: God and Jesus love us with real affection, not an abstract principle. For the disciple, to love Jesus is not an external obligation, but a response of the heart. Understanding this distinction between friendship and sincere affection helps to discern, like Peter, the difference between deep love and pretense.

sens: Who loves, who seeks pleasure
Who places pleasure above all, even God
G5369.detail:
1. The word designates one who loves, who actively seeks pleasure — not occasionally, but by inclination, by disposition of the heart. It is someone for whom the pursuit of pleasure is natural and habitual, just as it is for another person to be hospitable or generous.
2. In its biblical usage, it takes on a serious moral hue: one who loves pleasure more than God. In 2 Timothy 3:4, Paul describes the last days by listing moral faults, including this one: "lovers of pleasure more than lovers of God." It is the love of pleasure that becomes master, that takes precedence over the fear and obedience to God — a form of idolatry of personal well-being.
G5369.origine: The Greek word is composed of two roots: φίλος (philos, "friend of," "one who loves") and ἡδονή (hedone, "pleasure"). The image is that of a friendship for pleasure, of an affectionate closeness to it. The same root φίλος appears in common words like φιλόσοφος (philosopher, literally "friend of wisdom"). The word conveys a permanent disposition of the heart, not an isolated act.
G5369.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 3:4. Paul describes the characters of men in the last days: "lovers of pleasure more than lovers of God." In this context, "loving pleasure" does not condemn all desire for well-being — it denounces the one who, out of pride and selfishness, places his conveniences, his immediate satisfactions before obedience, piety, and relationship with God. It is a portrait of practical unbelief.
G5369.portee: This word challenges the Christian: it helps him discern the heart of idolatry. Loving pleasure "more than God" does not mean that the Christian must hate joy or well-being; it is a warning against the order of priorities — the one who puts God in the background to satisfy his desires. It reminds us that true faith reorders our affections and choices.

sens: Contact of the mouth on someone or something, gesture of affection or respect
Gesture of betrayal or false friendship
Fraternal greeting of welcome among Christians
Expression of love and communion among brothers and sisters in Christ
G5370.detail: 1. The kiss is primarily a simple physical gesture: one places their mouth on someone or something to express affection, respect, or love. When the sinful woman washes Jesus' feet, she covers them with kisses as a sign of gratitude and repentance (Luke 7:45). It is an intimate and sincere contact. 2. But the kiss can also become a gesture of deceit and betrayal: it is by a kiss that Judas delivers Jesus to the soldiers, transforming a sign of friendship into a signal of condemnation (Luke 22:48). The affectionate appearance hides a malevolent intention. 3. In the apostles' epistles, the kiss takes on a new ecclesial significance: it has become a rite of greeting at the heart of the life of the early Church. It is called the "holy kiss" (Romans 16:16, 1 Corinthians 16:20, 2 Corinthians 13:12, 1 Thessalonians 5:26), a liturgical act that seals the unity of God's people. 4. The kiss of love in 1 Peter 5:14 extends this meaning: it is not a mere worldly embrace, but the visible expression of fraternal charity and authentic communion that should prevail among Christ's disciples.
G5370.origine: The word φίλημα comes from the verb φιλέω, which means "to love" or "to kiss." Its root evokes the idea of affectionate and tender contact. In Hebrew, the word נְשִׁיקָה (nephikah) refers to both the physical kiss and a form of intimacy. Greek chooses to extend this simple gesture to the life of the Christian community, imbuing it with a new spiritual significance: the kiss becomes a word of the body in the Church.
G5370.emploi: The word kiss (φίλημα) appears 7 times in the New Testament. The first two occurrences in Luke are historical accounts: they show the kiss as a gesture of sincere affection (the sinful woman, Luke 7:45) or as infamous deceit (Judas, Luke 22:48). The other five appear in the apostolic letters as an order or encouragement for ecclesial practice: it is a greeting that Christians should give to one another during gatherings, thus sealing their unity and fraternal charity. The adjective "holy" or the specification "of love" (ἀγάπης) indicates that this kiss is not a mere social custom, but an act filled with spiritual meaning, distinct from a carnal or worldly kiss.
G5370.portee: The kiss teaches us that the body, our visible gestures, carry a profound spiritual and communal significance. In Judas, the kiss warns us that appearances of piety can mask betrayal; in the sinful woman, it reveals true repentance. For the Church, the kiss of peace reminds us that our communion in Christ must be expressed in concrete gestures of fraternity, welcome, and mutual honor. It is an invitation to transform every fraternal encounter into a moment of sanctification.

sens: Christian from Colossae, slave of Paul by faith
Master for whom Paul intercedes for the slave Onesimus
G5371.detail: Philemon is a Christian from the city of Colossae, who likely became a believer through Paul's ministry. Paul calls him his "beloved" and "fellow worker," which shows their close spiritual bond (Philemon 1:1). This wealthy man owned a slave named Onesimus who had run away; Paul, imprisoned, intercedes with Philemon on behalf of Onesimus, pleading with him to receive him no longer as a slave but as a "beloved brother" (Philemon 1:10-17). The entire epistle that bears his name is dedicated to this delicate and profound request.
G5371.origine: Philemon literally means "the one who loves" or "friend" in ancient Greek, from the verb φιλέω (philéō, to love). This personal name reflects the character of this man: a loving person, capable of the fraternal friendship that Paul asks him to extend to his converted slave.
G5371.emploi: Philemon is named twice in the New Testament, only in the epistle that bears his name (Philemon 1:1 and 1:25). He is a prosperous Christian from Colossae, a master of slaves, hospitable: Paul mentions that the saints gather in his house (Philemon 1:2). His importance lies less in his ecclesial notoriety than in his decisive role in this story of a converted slave and fraternal reconciliation, which constitutes one of the most beautiful biblical testimonies of the transformation that the Gospel brings to human relationships.
G5371.portee: The story of Philemon teaches the Christian reader that faith in Christ abolishes social barriers: master and slave become brothers in Christ. It is a call to lovingly welcome the one who was once separated from us, and to recognize in every convert a full member of the family of God, worthy of respect and affection.

sens: a first-century man who spread false doctrine in the Church
G5372.detail: Philetus is a character in the New Testament mentioned only once by Paul in his second letter to Timothy. He is a false teacher who, alongside Hymenaeus, taught a dangerous heresy: he claimed that the resurrection had already taken place (2 Timothy 2:18), thus deceiving believers about a fundamental truth of the Christian faith.
G5372.origine: The name Philetus comes from the ancient Greek φίλητος (philètos), which means "beloved" or "lovable" (from φιλέω, philéo, "to love").
