It is a common personal name in the Greco-Roman world. The irony may not be coincidental: one who bears a name meaning "beloved" has become an enemy of the evangelical truth.
G5372.emploi: Philetus appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 2:17-18. Paul mentions him as an example of a false teacher whose words "spread like gangrene." Together with Hymenaeus, he represents a major danger to the early Church: diverting believers from the hope of future resurrection by claiming it has already occurred. Paul delivers him to Satan as ultimate correction (1 Timothy 1:20 for Hymenaeus). He is a type of one who corrupts Christian doctrine through pride or false wisdom.
G5372.portee: The case of Philetus warns us that a seductive heresy — here, the idea that the resurrection has passed — can cause more damage than external persecution. His mention shows why Timothy must remain vigilant and faithful to sound doctrine: some abandon the faith not out of lack of courage, but by listening to false teachers. It is a call to discern between what is said about God and what is truly based on the Word.

sens: affection for temporal and earthly things
attachment to the values and pleasures that the world offers without God
opposition to the love of God
G5373.detail: 1. The word denotes the affection, friendship, love one has for someone or something — here, the heart's attachment to the realities of the world, its riches, honors, pleasures. 2. In James 4:4, the apostle speaks of "love of the world" to describe this deep attachment to earthly values: popularity, money, comfort, everything that society values without God. 3. This love of the world is not neutral: it places the one who nurtures it in hostility toward God, for it creates a rivalry: one cannot serve both the world and God with the same heart.
G5373.origine: The word comes from the root φίλ- (phil-) which expresses love in the sense of personal affection, deep friendship — different from absolute sacrificial love (agapè). Ancient Greek speaks of "philia" as the bond between friends. In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), it primarily translates the Hebrew ahavah (love). Here, James uses it to emphasize a heart attachment, a tenderness toward the world.
G5373.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible (James 4:4). The apostle James warns scattered Christians against the temptation to conform their lives to the values of the world: wealth, social status, comfort. He calls this emotional attachment "love of the world," which, in reality, constitutes unfaithfulness to God. It is a call to vigilance: one cannot both love the world in this way and be a friend of God.
G5373.portee: This word poses an inevitable question to the Christian: where does my heart truly go? Loving the things of the world — money, prestige, pleasures — is not neutral; it is taking a stand against God. James does not condemn the use of earthly goods, but the love that attaches to them. For the believer, it is an invitation to order one's affections: to put friendship with God first, and see all earthly goods as secondary.

sens: inhabitant or member of the church of Philippi, a city in Macedonia
G5374.detail: 1. Inhabitant of Philippi or Christian member of the church established in this city of northern Greece. The word specifically designates the believers of Philippi to whom Paul addresses his letter. In Philippians 4:15, Paul tells the "Philippians" that no church entered into partnership with him for giving and receiving at the beginning of his preaching of the Gospel, except for them who supported him financially in his mission.
G5374.origine: The word comes from Philippi (Φίλιπποι), the name of the city founded by Philip II of Macedonia (father of Alexander the Great), to which the suffix -ήσιος is added, forming an adjective or noun designating an inhabitant or citizen. It is a classical Greek formation to express belonging to a city.
G5374.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's letter to the Philippians. It is used to collectively designate the Christians of Philippi, a community founded by Paul during his second missionary journey (around 49-50 AD). This church was particularly attached to Paul and provided him with material support. The context shows the privileged relationship between Paul and this faithful community.
G5374.portee: This word reminds us that the early Church was composed of local communities with their own identity and strong ties to those who evangelized them. The Philippians exemplify generosity and faithfulness toward those who proclaim the Gospel, a model that encourages material support and prayers for those who serve the Lord.

sens: City of Macedonia in northern Greece
First Roman colony in this district
Site of Lydia's conversion and the jailer
Seat of a Church founded by Paul
G5375.detail:
1. Philippi is an important city in northern Greece, in the region of Macedonia. It is "the leading city of a district of Macedonia, and a Roman colony" (Acts 16:12), which means it was established to serve the interests of Rome.
2. Paul arrives there during his second missionary journey, called by the vision of a Macedonian man. There he meets Lydia, a seller of purple, and the jailer, both of whom become believers. It is also in Philippi that Paul and Silas are imprisoned and beaten "after suffering and being insulted" (1 Thessalonians 2:2).
3. From this encounter arises the Church of Philippi, composed of "saints in Christ Jesus" to whom Paul later addresses (Philippians 1:1). This Church becomes dear to Paul's heart.
G5375.origine: The name Philippi comes from King Philip II of Macedonia, father of Alexander the Great, who founded the city in the 4th century BC by enlarging an earlier Greek settlement. The name literally means "that of Philip" or "friend of horses" according to Greek etymology, although it is primarily the name of the founder that has prevailed.
G5375.emploi: Philippi appears four times in the New Testament, always associated with Paul. The first mention (Acts 16:12) situates it geographically and historically as a Roman colony. The two passages in Acts (16:12 and 20:6) recount the moments when Paul passed through or departed from it. The letter to the Philippians (1:1) shows that Paul writes to the Church established there. Finally, 1 Thessalonians 2:2 mentions the sufferings that Paul and Silas endured there for the Gospel. Together, these texts make it a center of Paul's ministry and a testimony of the establishment of the Church in the Greek world.
G5375.portee: Philippi symbolizes for the Christian reader the power of divine grace in the most distant places. It is where the Gospel reaches a new continent and creates a faithful community despite persecution. The story of Philippi reminds us that faith often arises at the cost of suffering, but it grows and endures through the faithfulness of God and His servants.

sens: Apostle of Christ, one of the twelve
The one who brings Nathanael to Jesus
The practical man who thinks of concrete needs
The one who wants to see Jesus face to face
Brother in Christ and faithful disciple
G5376G.detail:
1. Philip is one of the twelve apostles that Jesus chose to follow Him and carry His message (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14). He accompanies Jesus in His travels and witnesses His miracles and teachings.

2. It is Philip who meets Nathanael and invites him to follow Jesus by simply saying, "Come and see" (John 1:46). This phrase shows how he shares his faith with others.

3. When a large hungry crowd surrounds Jesus, Philip is the one who asks the practical question: "Where shall we buy bread?" (John 6:5). He thinks of the real needs of the people, the logistical problem — a very human reaction.

4. At the last supper, Philip asks Jesus, "Lord, show us the Father" (John 14:8). He expresses the deep desire to truly know God, directly.

5. Philip is from Bethsaida in Galilee (John 1:44), the same city as Peter and Andrew. He remains a loyal disciple throughout Jesus' ministry and after the Resurrection (Acts 1:13).
G5376G.origine: The name Philip comes from Greek and means "friend of horses" (from "philos," friend, and "hippos," horse) — but this Greek meaning does not shed much light on the biblical character. In the New Testament, it is simply the name borne by this apostle. This name was also held by two Herodian kings (the husband of Herodias and the tetrarch), but they are not the same Philip as the apostle.
G5376G.emploi: Philip is named in all lists of the apostles (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13). The Gospel of John speaks of him more: it shows him bringing Nathanael to Jesus (John 1:44-46), asking a practical question during the feeding of the 5,000 (John 6:5), serving as an intermediary when Greeks want to meet Jesus (John 12:21-22), and expressing his desire to see the Father (John 14:8-9). He is not the most prominent apostle: he is a simple, practical, faithful man who accompanies Jesus without particularly shining.
G5376G.portee: Philip represents the ordinary and faithful disciple, one who acts quietly: he brings others to Jesus, thinks of concrete needs, and asks the right questions. His example teaches that the Christian faith does not need to be spectacular to be true. It also shows that even after following Jesus for three years, one can still seek to know Him more — his request "show us the Father" expresses a thirst for greater intimacy with God.

sens: Brother of Herod the tetrarch, husband of Herodias
The tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis
G5376H.detail:
1. Philip was the brother of Herod Antipas, the tetrarch (governor of a region) who imprisoned and then executed John the Baptist. Philip had been married to Herodias, but Herod Antipas took her as his wife (Matthew 14:3, Mark 6:17). It was for marrying his brother's wife that John the Baptist reproached Herod, which provoked his vengeance.
2. Another Philip, son of Herod the Great, was tetrarch (governor) of Iturea and Trachonitis, a region north of Galilee (Luke 3:1). He should not be confused with his brother Herod Antipas.
G5376H.origine: The Greek name Philippos means "friend of horses" (philos = friend, hippos = horse). It is a common royal name in the Herodian family. In the Bible, this name designates several distinct historical figures from the Herodian dynasty and disciples of Jesus.
G5376H.emploi: The term "Philip" designates several people in the New Testament. The provided usages concern two members of the Herodian family: first, Philip, brother of Herod Antipas and husband of Herodias (Matthew 14:3, Mark 6:17), whose irregular marriage provoked the reproaches of John the Baptist; then Philip the tetrarch, brother of Herod Antipas, who governed Iturea and Trachonitis (Luke 3:1). The Bible also mentions two apostles named Philip and a deacon-evangelist of the same name, but the references here concern the two Herodian princes.
G5376H.portee: These passages remind us how Herod's personal sin — taking his brother's wife — made him hostile to the word of God proclaimed by John the Baptist. For the Christian, it is a lesson on the cost of moral justice and the importance of listening to God's messengers, even when their message accuses us.

sens: Herod Philip, tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis
Son of Herod the Great, brother of Herod Antipas
Governor of a part of the territories east of the Jordan under Roman authority
G5376I.detail: 1. Herod Philip was a son of Herod the Great and one of the tetrarchs (governors of small territories) of the Levant during the time of Jesus. He ruled over Iturea and Trachonitis, regions located east of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee, as indicated by the enumeration in Luke 3:1, which places him alongside Pontius Pilate and his brother Herod Antipas.
G5376I.origine: The name "Philip" (Philippos in Greek) literally means "friend of horses" (from phileô, to love, and hippos, horse). It is a Greek name borne by several biblical characters, including apostles of Jesus. Here, it designates one of the sons of King Herod the Great, who ruled in the first half of the first century AD.
G5376I.emploi: Herod Philip is mentioned in the New Testament as tetrarch of a Palestinian region at the time of Jesus' ministry. He is the brother of Herod Antipas (the one who had John the Baptist executed). Luke 3:1 situates him historically in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, placing his reign in a specific political context of Roman domination in Judea. Unlike his brothers, Philip is presented in historical sources as a relatively just and peaceful governor.

sens: One of the twelve apostles of Jesus
The deacon and evangelist of the early Church
G5376J.detail:
1. Philip is one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. He comes from Bethsaida and it is he whom Jesus meets near the Jordan and says to, "Follow me" (John 1:44-49). At the table during the last supper, Philip asks Jesus to show them the Father, which reveals his desire to see and know God Himself (John 14:8-9).

2. Philip is also one of the seven men "full of faith and the Holy Spirit" that the assembly of believers in Jerusalem elected to distribute aid to the widows (Acts 6:5). Later, he becomes a great evangelist: he preaches powerfully in Samaria, baptizes the Ethiopian eunuch on his way to Gaza, and the Spirit guides him at every step of his testimony (Acts 8:5-40). The Bible shows him being directly guided by the Holy Spirit, who tells him, "Go, and join this chariot" (Acts 8:29).
G5376J.origine: The name "Philip" comes from Greek and literally means "friend of horses" (from *philos* = friend and *hippos* = horse). It is a common Greek name in antiquity, borne by several important figures, including the king of Macedonia, father of Alexander the Great. In the New Testament, this name designates at least four different people: two apostles, a prince, and a deacon.
G5376J.emploi: Philip appears 16 times in the New Testament, mostly concentrated in the Gospel of John and the book of Acts. In the Gospels, he is a discreet yet significant apostle: he is named in the lists of the twelve (Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14), and John shows him in personal interaction with Jesus, presenting him to Nathanael and asking the great question of the heart: "Show us the Father." In Acts, he truly shines: elected as a deacon in Jerusalem (Acts 6:5), he becomes a powerful preacher and miracle worker in Samaria (Acts 8:6-13), then the Holy Spirit leads him to the road to Gaza where he meets and baptizes the Ethiopian eunuch — a key passage in the spreading of the Church beyond Israel (Acts 8:26-40). His ministry shows the transition of the early Church from material service to evangelization.
G5376J.portee: Philip teaches believers that intimacy with Jesus is not passively given: it requires daring to ask questions ("Show us the Father"). His example in Acts also shows how the Holy Spirit concretely guides those who are available — the Spirit tells him where to go, when to move forward, when to stop — and how a faithful servant grows from humble responsibilities (distributing aid) to an extraordinary ministry of evangelization. He is a model of flexible obedience to God's direction.

sens: Region of Macedonia (Northern Greece)
G5376K.detail: Caesarea Philippi is a city located in the northeast of the Mediterranean basin, in Macedonia. It is near this city that Jesus asks his disciples the pivotal question: "Who do people say that I am?" (Matthew 16:13, Mark 8:27). The name "Philip" comes from King Herod Philip, who renamed it.
G5376K.origine: The Greek name Philippos means "friend of horses" (philos = friend, hippos = horse). At the time of the New Testament, it refers to the region that the tetrarch Herod Philip developed and named in his honor.
G5376K.emploi: The New Testament mentions Caesarea Philippi twice, in the two parallel passages where Matthew and Mark report that Jesus went there with his disciples. It is a strategic location, well-known at the time, situated near the springs of the Jordan. It is there that Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah.
G5376K.portee: This place marks a major turning point in the Gospel: it is the starting point of Jesus' teaching about his Church and the revelation of the Father to the believer. Mentioning the tetrarch Herod in the name of the city anchors the narrative in the concrete history of first-century Galilee.

sens: one who loves God
one who is devoted to God through piety
G5377.detail:
1. One who loves God: this is the literal meaning of the Greek word, formed from two elements meaning "friend" and "God." It is the person who has affection for God, who places their love in Him, as one would love a friend. In 2 Timothy 3:4, Paul lists the faults of the last days and highlights this one: men will be "lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God" — the opposite of being a friend of God.
2. One who is devoted to God through piety: beyond feeling, it is a disposition of the heart that manifests itself through faithfulness, obedience, and fear of God. The friend of God seeks to please Him and to live according to His will.
G5377.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and combines two roots: "philo-" (friend, one who loves) and "theos" (God). It is a compound that expresses the orientation of the heart towards God. Related words include "philosophy" (love of wisdom) and "philanthropy" (love of humanity). This Greek formation conveys the biblical idea of a loving and obedient communion with the Lord.
G5377.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:4. Paul paints a picture of the difficult times of the end of the ages, where people will be selfish, lovers of themselves and of pleasure. In this enumeration of vices, he contrasts those who love pleasure with those who would love God — emphasizing a radical choice between two loves. The absence of a friend of God among the listed vices underscores that it is the opposite virtue: a life devoted to God rather than to carnal desires.
G5377.portee: This word reminds Christians that loving God is not a cold obligation, but a relationship of friendship — a sincere affection towards the Creator. In a time when the world cultivates love for pleasure and self, the friend of God chooses to orient their heart towards the One who knows and loves them. It is a call to reassess our priorities: to place the love of God above all worldly pleasures.

sens: Christian from Rome greeted by Paul in his letter to the Romans
G5378.detail: Philologus is a Christian man living in Rome at the time Paul writes his letter to the Romans. Paul greets him by name, alongside Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympas, and other believers. This simple greeting shows that he was a respected member of the Roman Christian assembly.
G5378.origine: The Greek name Philologos is composed of two elements: "philo" (love) and "logos" (word, or knowledge). It literally means "friend of the word" or "friend of knowledge." It was a common name in the Greco-Roman world to designate someone who was educated or cultured. The name reflects the ancient ideal of one who loves to learn and discuss.
G5378.emploi: Philologus appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:15, in Paul's final greetings. Paul mentions this man among the believers in Rome whom he knows personally or has heard about. His inclusion in this particular enumeration suggests that he was a trustworthy Christian and likely an active servant in the local church.
G5378.portee: The simple fact that Paul greets Philologus by name shows that in the early church, Christians recognized and honored those who stood out for their faith and commitment. This reminds us of the importance of personally encouraging our brothers and sisters in Christ and acknowledging their service, even if our knowledge of them remains limited.

sens: Tendency to seek dispute, to want to be right at all costs
Rivalry, competition between people to obtain the first place
Quarrel, heated debate where each defends their point of view
G5379.detail:
1. It is the desire to dispute, to contradict, to not accept what the other says — the urge to win an argument. The Greek word combines "friend of" (philos) and "quarrel" (neike). We see this in Luke 22:24: the apostles dispute over who is the greatest; it is a contention born of ambition, not a true search for truth.
2. More broadly, it is a rivalry, an emulation where each wants to surpass the other, to show that they are better. This can be neutral (sports competition), but here in the Bible, it is always depicted as bad: one seeks to crush the other, not to improve oneself.
3. In a concrete sense, it is the quarrel that breaks out publicly: bitter words, accusations, the tense atmosphere of conflict. In Luke 22:24, it is a real "contention" that arises among the apostles at Jesus' meal.
G5379.origine: The word is formed from the root "philos" (friend, one who loves) and "neike" (quarrel, rivalry). It literally means "love of quarrel." This construction shows how Greek expresses faults: not as an absence of good, but as a misdirected passion — the love we naturally have, put to the service of dispute instead of unity.
G5379.emploi: The word appears only once in Greek in the New Testament, in Luke 22:24. It is during the Last Supper, when Jesus is sitting with the twelve apostles. A "contention" arises among them: they ask who should be considered the greatest. It is one of the moments where the disciples show their deep misunderstanding of Jesus' message — not only do they dispute, but they do so precisely when Jesus is about to give Himself for them. The context shows that this spirit of contention is a form of pride, of carnal ambition.
G5379.portee: This word confronts us with a common temptation among believers: wanting to be right, defending one's prestige, seeking the first place. Jesus responds to this contention by saying that the greatest among you should be like the least (Luke 22:26). The Holy Spirit calls for humility, for peace in the Church, for renouncing our need to shine. It is a word of warning: the spirit of contention is the opposite of brotherly love.

sens: One who loves to argue and always seeks to dispute
Prone to contradiction and fruitless debates
More concerned with being right than seeking peace
G5380.detail:
1. The word designates someone who naturally loves to argue and cannot help but contest — not out of deep conviction, but out of a taste for conflict. In 1 Corinthians 11:16, Paul says, "if anyone is inclined to be contentious," which refers to this spirit that finds pleasure in endlessly arguing about customs and practices.
2. It is less about a specific quarrel than a character disposition: the quarrelsome person systematically seeks disagreement, even on minor points. Their reflex is to combat the accepted opinion, not out of a sincere search for truth, but out of a love for verbal combat.
3. Paul contrasts this attitude with the habit of the Churches of God: it is a behavior that Christians must reject, as it disrupts the unity and peace that Christ calls for His people.
G5380.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "philos" (friend, one who loves) and "neikos" (dispute, quarrel, contention). The starting image is therefore "friend of dispute," someone who cherishes conflict. It is the temperament opposite to that of the peacemaker praised in Scripture.
G5380.emploi: The word appears only once in 1 Corinthians 11:16, in an exhortation from Paul to the Corinthians. They, being divided and quarrelsome, needed to hear that this spirit of perpetual contention does not correspond to how the churches of God operate. Paul uses it to qualify a negative spiritual attitude that needs correction.
G5380.portee: This word invites the believer to examine their heart: am I someone who loves peace and harmony, or am I prone to dispute for the sake of disputing? Jesus blesses those who bring peace. Fruitless quarrels, a spirit of contradiction, and a desire to be right are all signs of a flesh not submitted to the Spirit. It is a call to cultivate humility and a sincere pursuit of unity in the body of Christ.

sens: Welcoming reception of the traveler or stranger
Offering meals and lodging to one who comes from afar
Sharing one's table and home with the needy
Act of charity towards someone unknown
G5381.detail:
1. It is love manifested towards one who comes from afar and whom one does not know. The Greek word combines "friend" and "stranger": it precisely designates this attitude of warmth towards the traveler or migrant. In Romans 12:13, the Apostle Paul exhorts Christians to "practice hospitality," meaning to concretely engage in this welcoming.
2. It is expressed through specific gestures: offering a meal, providing shelter, meeting the material needs of the one passing through. In Hebrews 13:2, the text reminds us that "some have entertained angels unaware" — not that one should expect to host an angel, but that hospitality towards the unknown is of such great value that it may, without one knowing, concern celestial beings.
3. It is not a luxury, but an obligation of Christian conscience: it is among the commandments Paul addresses to the Romans alongside helping the poor and sharing resources. It manifests love for one's neighbor without calculating for return.
G5381.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and combines φίλος (friend, one who loves) and ξένος (stranger, guest). In Hebrew, hospitality is called גרות ("gerout," from the verb "to welcome the stranger"): it is a fundamental virtue of the Law and the patriarchs, who eagerly welcomed the traveler. The concept is universal in ancient cultures, but the New Testament makes it a specific marker of Christian charity.
G5381.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, indicating that it is a precise and solemn term. In Romans 12:13, Paul includes hospitality in a list of virtues that the community must practice: it is a concrete duty of the body of Christ. In Hebrews 13:2, the author roots it in the tradition of the patriarchs — Abraham, Lot, and Job are famous for having welcomed visitors who turned out to be messengers of God — and elevates it to the level of a sacred act, without ever knowing who one is truly receiving. These two passages show that hospitality is neither passive nor occasional: it is an active and vigilant charity.
G5381.portee: For today's Christian, hospitality is a call to see Christ in the stranger, the migrant, the one who has nowhere to stay. It breaks indifference, creates a bond of trust and dignity, and bears witness to the love received from God. In a time of closure and mistrust, it is a prophetic practice: it says that faith does not confine itself at home, but generously opens up to those we do not know.

sens: One who loves to receive strangers and travelers
One who generously offers shelter and food to those who come from afar
One who kindly welcomes those unknown
G5382.detail: 1. The word hospitable primarily designates one who naturally loves to receive strangers and travelers — it is a disposition of the heart before being an action. This is why Paul asks that the bishop be hospitable: it is a moral quality, a character trait that shows the generosity of the one who leads (1 Timothy 3:2). 2. In concrete terms, being hospitable means generously offering shelter and a meal to those who come from afar, without expecting a reward. In biblical times, roads were dangerous and inns were rare or expensive: welcoming a traveler or a stranger is to save their life and show the love of Christ. 3. More broadly, hospitality is a moral virtue that church leaders must practice towards all, without murmuring or complaining (1 Peter 4:9): it is the art of joyfully and kindly welcoming those unknown, giving them what one has.
G5382.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: *philo-* (to love) and *xenos* (the stranger, the guest). It literally means "friend of the stranger." This composition reveals the essence of biblical hospitality: it is not an imposed duty, but a spontaneous love for one who comes from outside. The same root *xenos* is found in words like *xenodocheion* (inn), showing that hospitality was a vital need in the ancient world.
G5382.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to describe a quality of leaders and believers. In 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:8, Paul requires it of bishops and elders: it is a mark of their pastoral character and love for their neighbor. In 1 Peter 4:9, Peter broadens the call to all believers, urging them to practice hospitality towards one another. The emphasis on "without murmuring" shows that hospitality should not be a felt obligation, but a free and joyful practice. It is a rare and precious virtue: it requires time, money, and an open heart.
G5382.portee: Hospitality reveals Christian love in action. To receive the stranger, the one unknown, is to recognize the image of Christ in them and to live the Gospel concretely. This virtue also protects the body of the church: it creates bonds, supports travelers, and bears witness to faith in the world. For the believer today, it invites opening one's home and heart, not out of duty or for show, but out of true love for those who hunger for welcome.

sens: To eagerly seek to occupy the first place, the highest rank
To manifest an obsessive desire for precedence and personal honor
To refuse to submit to an established authority or hierarchy
G5383.detail:
1. The verb describes an ambition that actively seeks the first place: it is the desire to dominate, to command, to be recognized as the most important. In Diotrephes in 3 John 9, this is manifested by his refusal to receive the apostle John and his messengers: he wants to remain the undisputed authority of his assembly.
2. This quest for the first place reveals a heart attached to its own honor rather than to that of Christ and the Church. It is a self-love that takes precedence over unity and brotherly welcome.
3. The word stands in opposition to the humility and servitude that Jesus teaches: where the desire to be first reigns, the spirit of community and the communion of saints disappears.
G5383.origine: The word combines two Greek roots: "philos" (to love, to cherish) and "proteuō" (to be first, to hold the highest rank). It is a rare compound verb, forged to designate a specific passion: not merely ambition, but a possessive love for the first place. The root "protos" is found in words like "prototype" or "protocolar."
G5383.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 3 John 9, where it characterizes Diotrephes. Its uniqueness emphasizes that John is targeting this particular disposition of the heart: a desire not only to be important but to love that importance, to enjoy it, and to make it an idol. In the context of the young Church, this behavior threatens apostolic authority and the welcome of the community.
G5383.portee: This word challenges the believer regarding their own motivations: do they sincerely love the Church and their Lord, or do they secretly seek to hold a preeminent role within it? The warning concerning Diotrephes invites everyone to examine whether their heart truly loves the first place, whether in a hidden or manifest way. It is a call to humility and submission to the order that God establishes in His body.

sens: A person with whom one has a relationship of trust and affection
One who loves, who is kind
Companion for meals or daily life
Political or social ally
One who is loved by God
G5384.detail: 1. A friend is a person with whom one shares trust, affection, and intimacy. Jesus says to His disciples: "I no longer call you servants, but I have called you friends" (John 15:15), marking a relationship based on mutual knowledge and love, far beyond mere duty. 2. The word also designates one who loves or acts with kindness. Jesus is presented as "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" (Matthew 11:19): He shows affection towards those whom society rejects. 3. A friend can be someone with whom one shares meals and ordinary moments of life. The parable of the persistent friend features a friend who arrives at midnight after a journey and asks for food (Luke 11:5-8). 4. The word also takes on a political or diplomatic nuance: Pilate is concerned about not being accused of not being "a friend of Caesar" (John 19:12), meaning faithful and loyal to the established power. 5. In biblical language, friendship with God is an exceptional grace: Abraham is called "the friend of God" (James 2:23), designating one who lives in confident obedience and communion with Him.
G5384.origine: The Greek word φίλος comes from a root meaning "to love" and "to cherish." It regularly translates the Hebrew רֵעַ (friend, companion) and אָהַב (to love). The word family includes forms like φιλέω (to love, to cherish) and φιλία (friendship). The Greek term emphasizes personal feeling and affective relationship, distinguishing the friend from the mere acquaintance or servant.
G5384.emploi: The word φίλος appears 26 times in the Gospels and Epistles of the New Testament, especially in Luke, who loves to show conviviality and social relationships. It primarily designates ordinary companions: friends invited to a table (Luke 14:12), friends with whom one shares life (Luke 11:5). But Jesus elevates the meaning: He calls His disciples "friends" (John 15:13-15), establishing a friendship based on obedience and sacrificial love. The word takes on a theological significance when Abraham becomes "the friend of God" (James 2:23) or when a disciple of Jesus must renounce the friendship of the world (James 4:4). It can also qualify a political or functional relationship, as Herod and Pilate become "friends" (Luke 23:12).
G5384.portee: Jesus transforms the notion of friendship: it is no longer based on interest or social status, but on true love and unconditional acceptance. The disciple of Jesus is called to become His friend by obeying and loving Him, which radically changes the relationship with Him: from servant, one becomes confident. This divine friendship offers the believer an intimacy and security that surpass any human friendship, and it calls them to live this same quality of love towards others.

sens: The love and pursuit of wisdom
A form of teaching that claims to explain truth and the nature of things
A system of thought based on human tradition rather than on Christ
G5385.detail:
1. In a broad sense, philosophy is the love of wisdom and the quest for truth — this is what the Greek word literally says: "love of wisdom." It is an investigation of deep realities and the nature of the world.
2. The Bible uses this word to designate any teaching that presents itself as a path to wisdom or understanding, particularly that which relies on human traditions and general principles (referred to as "elements of the world"). In Colossians 2:8, Paul warns against such a "philosophy" that circulates among the converts.
3. In this context, philosophy becomes a seduction: it appears to be a path of truth, but it diverts from the true foundation, which is Christ. Paul describes it as "empty deceit" — a system that dazzles with its appearances but leads only to emptiness and confusion.
G5385.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and is composed of two roots: "philo-" (to love) and "sophia" (wisdom). It is thus literally the love and pursuit of wisdom. The French word "philosophie" is a direct heir of this. In Greek thought, it was a noble and respectable activity; but Paul takes it up to show that some use the prestige of the name to promote doctrines that contradict the Gospel.
G5385.emploi: The word "philosophy" appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 2:8. Paul uses it to criticize a set of teachings that were circulating among the church in Colossae. These teachers claimed to lead to spiritual perfection through adherence to rules, observance of ritual practices, and asceticism, while relying on human tradition rather than on the revelation of Christ. Paul does not condemn wisdom itself, but false wisdom that adorns itself with the trappings of philosophy to lead believers away from Christ, who is "the hidden treasure of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3).
G5385.portee: This passage teaches the Christian to remain vigilant against any system of thought — even if it is seductive and seemingly wise — that would divert their heart from Christ and the Gospel. True wisdom is not human speculation, but the living knowledge of Jesus Christ. The believer should not reject intelligence or reflection, but submit them to biblical revelation and to Him in whom all wisdom resides.

sens: a man who dedicates himself to the love and pursuit of wisdom
a thinker who offers an explanation of the world and life according to his doctrine
sophist or orator who debates in public places
G5386.detail:
1. A philosopher is literally a "friend of wisdom": he is a man who seeks to understand the nature of all things and to live according to reason. The term primarily refers to one who cultivates this passion for knowledge and proposes principles for living well, like the Epicureans and Stoics mentioned in Acts 17:18, each having their own vision of happiness and virtue.
2. By extension, the philosopher is one who publicly presents his doctrine and engages in dialogue on great questions. In Athens, he is a figure in public debate, a thinker who argues and discusses in public spaces to convince other minds.
G5386.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "friend" (philos) of "wisdom" (sophia). It is a compound formation that expresses the love of wisdom, characterizing one who makes it his quest. The term does not exist in biblical Hebrew, as the Greek thought of wisdom acquired through reason was foreign to Israelite culture.
G5386.emploi: The word appears only once in Acts 17:18, during Paul's stay in Athens. In this passage, Paul encounters Epicurean and Stoic philosophers who question him about his new doctrine concerning Jesus and the resurrection. The context shows thinkers engaged in public debate, intrigued by this announcer of a message they find strange. This unique occurrence reflects the encounter between the Christian gospel and the purely rational wisdom of Greek paganism.
G5386.portee: This encounter between Paul and the philosophers of Athens reminds the reader that the Christian faith is not a mere human philosophy based on reason, but a revelation from God that surpasses the wisdom of the world. It invites recognition that the answers to the greatest questions do not come from human reflection alone, but from listening to the Word of God and faith in the resurrection of Christ.

sens: who loves with tenderness and devotion
who shows deep and natural affection
characterized by familial love and mutual kindness
G5387.detail:
1. This word describes a person who loves with a natural and sincere tenderness, as in a close family. It is the affection of the heart that is openly expressed, without coldness or calculation — the kind that drives family members to be attentive and kind to one another.

2. As an adjective, it qualifies an attitude of practical and generous love towards others. When Paul exhorts the Romans to be "full of affection for one another" (Romans 12:10), he asks them to cultivate this fraternal tenderness within the Church, just as one would love their own relatives.
G5387.origine: The word is formed from "storgè," which denotes natural affection, particularly that which unites family members. It is a love rooted in nature, spontaneous and enduring, distinct from other forms of love that are more passionate or calculated. This root evokes the image of daily tenderness, manifested in gestures and mutual attentions.
G5387.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 12:10. Paul uses it to urge the Christians in Rome to maintain sincere fraternal affection among themselves, at the heart of his description of communal love in the Church. The context shows that this affection must be accompanied by mutual honor and deference: it is not a mere emotion, but a disposition of the heart expressed through concrete acts of consideration and kindness.
G5387.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that love in the Church is not a cold or abstract obligation, but should spring from real tenderness, like that of a family. It is a call to cultivate sincere affection for our brothers and sisters in Christ, to honor them and be attentive to their needs, not out of mere duty, but from a heartfelt attachment.

sens: Who loves their children with tenderness
Who shows affection towards their offspring
G5388.detail: 1. The word designates a person, particularly a woman, who loves her children with natural affection and kindness. It is the love of a parent for their child, expressed through tenderness and devotion. In Titus 2:4, Paul encourages young women to cultivate this love for their children, a virtue that characterizes a mother's heart.
G5388.origine: The word is composed of two simple Greek roots: "phílos" (friend, one who loves) and "tékton" (child). This composition conveys the basic idea of one who loves children. Tenderness towards offspring is a virtue recognized in ancient Greek wisdom (Herodotus, Aristotle, Plutarch) long before the New Testament.
G5388.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Titus 2:4. Paul uses it while listing the qualities that older women should teach to younger women. It appears alongside "philandros" (loving their husbands), forming a pair of essential domestic virtues. It is a rare but clear word, without particular nuance according to the passages.
G5388.portee: This verse reminds Christians, particularly mothers, that the love for children is not a biological inevitability, but a virtue to be consciously cultivated. It is an invitation to transform natural affection into thoughtful, attentive, and generous love, reflecting the love with which God surrounds His spiritual children.

sens: Seeking to obtain honor, consideration, glory
Showing ambition and zeal for a cause or a person
Striving earnestly to accomplish something noble or important
G5389.detail: 1. The word first describes one who runs after honor and consideration, who wants to be esteemed and recognized (Romans 15:20: Paul takes pride in preaching the Gospel where Christ was not known). 2. It also expresses generous ambition, sincere zeal: not a hollow vanity, but a burning desire to serve a worthy cause or person (2 Corinthians 5:9: we strive to please God). 3. Finally, it is the voluntary effort, the resolution to do something good with dedication (1 Thessalonians 4:11: to make it a point to live quietly and work with one's hands).
G5389.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: φίλος (philos, friend, one who loves) and τιμή (timè, honor, price, esteem). It literally means "to love honor." The family of the word includes φιλονεικέομαι (to seek to win, to compete) and other verbs ending in -έομαι that express aspirations or desires.
G5389.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always in Paul’s writings and always to describe a mature and thoughtful personal aspiration. In Romans 15:20, Paul speaks of his honor in preaching where Christ has not been named: it is the ambition of an apostle guided by God's vision. In 2 Corinthians 5:9, aspiring to please God becomes the deep motivation of the Christian life. In 1 Thessalonians 4:11, Paul places work and modest living among the honorable things worthy of effort. The meaning varies according to the complement: one can aspire to the honor of God, to please God, or to live honorably.
G5389.portee: This word reminds Christians that ambition is not a sin when it is well-directed: aspiring to honor God, to please Him, to serve His Gospel, to live honorably from the fruit of one's labor—these are noble and commendable ambitions. Paul depicts it as a healthy driving force in the life of faith, opposed to idleness and selfishness.

sens: Manner of receiving someone with warmth and friendship
Warm and generous welcome
G5390.detail:
1. This word describes the manner in which one receives someone: with a kind heart, true human warmth. In Acts 28:7, Publius receives Paul and his companions "in the most friendly manner" after a shipwreck: it is a gesture of spontaneous and sincere hospitality, not mere formal politeness.

2. More broadly, it is the attitude of one who opens their home with generosity and affection, treating the stranger or traveler as a friend. The adverb emphasizes that it is not out of obligation, but from a feeling of true friendship.
G5390.origine: The word comes from φιλόφρων (philophron), composed of φιλέω (philéō, "to love") and φρήν (phrēn, "heart" or "mind"). Literally, it means "one who has a loving heart." In Greek, this root appears in several words related to affection and hospitality. It is a rare word in the New Testament, emphasizing sincere feelings rather than mere actions.
G5390.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 28:7, where it describes the welcome that Publius, the chief of the island of Malta, gives to Paul and his companions after their shipwreck. In this context of a difficult journey, the adverb emphasizes that Publius does not merely provide lodging: he receives them with sincere friendship. It is a moment of grace where, despite the circumstances, a pagan stranger shows generosity and kindness toward the Christian missionary.
G5390.portee: This scene reminds us that true hospitality is not merely a social duty, but a heartfelt impulse. For the believer, it invites us to receive others, especially strangers and those in need, with sincerity and warmth that reflect the love of Christ. It also shows that kindness can come from someone who does not know the Gospel, and that it is a virtue that God honors.

sens: To muzzle an animal to prevent it from eating or making noise
To impose silence on someone or a spirit; to forbid speech
To remain silent, keeping quiet despite oneself
G5392.detail:
1. In its primary sense, it means to put a muzzle on the mouth of a beast to gag it: the image comes from the Greek phimós (muzzle). This is why Paul cites Deuteronomy 25:4 saying "You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain" (1 Corinthians 9:9), which gives the etymology of the word.

2. In a figurative sense, it means to forcibly impose silence on someone, forbidding them to speak. When Jesus threatens a demoniac by saying "Be silent" (Mark 1:25, Luke 4:35), he uses this verb to force it to come out of the man without making noise. The Pharisees, having seen Jesus "silence" the Sadducees (Matthew 22:34), understand that he has shut them up with irresistible arguments.

3. The passive form, "to be silenced," describes the state of one who cannot or should not speak. The man without the wedding garment "was speechless" (Matthew 22:12), condemned to be unable to respond. In Mark 4:39, Jesus says to the wind and the sea, "Peace! Be still!", giving orders with this same absolute authority.
G5392.origine: The word comes from phimós, which literally means muzzle or gag. It is a concrete word, probably borrowed from an ancient language to describe the act of muzzling animals. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew hasam (חָסַם) in the sense of gagging or muzzling. The word always retains this image of a gag: to impose silence on someone is to muzzle them like an animal one wants to dominate or control.
G5392.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. In its literal sense, Paul uses it once for the Mosaic law (1 Corinthians 9:9). In its figurative sense, it becomes very common: Jesus uses it to command demons (Mark 1:25, Luke 4:35) and even natural forces (Mark 4:39), showing his sovereign authority over all spirits. Matthew uses it to describe how Jesus "silences" his opponents in debate (Matthew 22:34), or how a man remains mute in confusion (Matthew 22:12). Peter speaks of it in a moral sense: silencing the ignorance of foolish men by good conduct (1 Peter 2:15).
G5392.portee: This word reveals the absolute authority of Jesus: it is so powerful that it imposes silence even on demons and the forces of nature. For the believer, it shows that God controls everything, even imposing silence on what opposes his reign. It is also an invitation to restraint: knowing when to be silent, in the face of divine wisdom, is to recognize his authority.

sens: man from Rome in the 1st century, member of the Christian community
G5393.detail: Phlegon is a Christian from Rome mentioned only once in the New Testament. Paul personally greets him in his letter to the Romans, indicating that he was known and esteemed by the apostle despite the distance that separated them. His name, which literally means "burning" in Greek, was quite common in the Roman Empire.
G5393.origine: The name Phlegon comes from the Greek verb phlegō (to burn), expressing the idea of flame or fire. This type of name, formed on an image of heat or passion, was popular in the Greco-Roman world. The meaning of the name suggests a certain fervor, although we do not know if this reflected the actual character of the individual.
G5393.emploi: Phlegon appears only in Romans 16:14, in the list of personal greetings that Paul addresses to various people in the Christian community of Rome. He is mentioned alongside Asyncritus, Hermes, Patrobas, and Hermas, as well as the brothers who accompany them. This brief mention suggests that he was an established Christian in Rome, known to Paul and part of those groups of disciples to whom the apostle wishes to convey a message of brotherhood and affection.

sens: To set fire to, to blaze
To excite, to animate with a burning passion
G5394.detail:
1. To set fire to, to blaze: this is the literal sense of the verb, evoking a flame that ignites and spreads. In James 3:6, the apostle compares the tongue to a fire that "ignites the course of life": just as a spark can set an entire house ablaze, a word can destroy a person's existence.
2. To excite, to animate with a burning passion: by extension, the verb denotes the action of igniting a passion, anger, or desire in someone's heart. In the same verse, the tongue itself is "set on fire by hell," meaning it is driven by a destructive and malevolent force.
G5394.origine: The verb comes from the Greek word φλόξ (phlox), which means flame or fire. Its basic image is that of fire igniting and spreading. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew verbs that also evoke fire and burning, such as לָהַט (lahát, "to blaze") in Psalm 97:3. It is a concrete word that refers to the tangible reality of combustion before being used to describe emotions and moral forces.
G5394.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in James 3:6, in the context of the famous passage about the tongue. James deploys a series of fire images to show the destructive power of speech: the tongue is "a fire," it "ignites the course of life," it is itself "set on fire by hell." This passage uses both the literal and figurative sense of the verb to highlight how words can destroy, corrupt, and cause lasting harm to those who hear them and to the one who utters them.
G5394.portee: This word reminds the Christian of the formidable power of their words. Like fire that spreads quickly and destroys everything in its path, an impulsive or malevolent word can cause deep and lasting wounds. This invites vigilance and control over one's tongue, knowing that our words are never without spiritual and moral consequence.

sens: Visible tongue of fire that rises from a hearth
Intense and burning light that radiates
Image of anger, judgment, or divine power
Brilliant manifestation of the presence or nature of God
G5395.detail:
1. A flame is primarily that trait of fire that one sees rising from a hearth, with its color and heat — this is the most concrete sense of the word. In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, the rich man asks Father Abraham to send Lazarus to "dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue; for I am in anguish in this flame" (Luke 16:24): he speaks of the flame as the burning reality of the place of torment.
2. The flame also refers to the intense and incandescent light that emanates from fire. In the vision of the burning bush, Moses sees "an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush" (Acts 7:30): it is the bright clarity that radiates from the blazing bush.
3. The flame becomes an image of divine power and presence. When the epistle to the Hebrews cites: "He makes his angels winds, And his ministers a flame of fire" (Hebrews 1:7), it speaks of angels as fiery servants of God, displaying a burning energy and liveliness.
4. In John and Revelation, the flame symbolizes the divinity of Christ and his judgment. "His eyes were like a flame of fire" (Revelation 1:14; 2:18; 19:12) expresses the total penetration of the gaze of the risen and glorified Christ, who scrutinizes all things and against whom nothing can hide.
G5395.origine: The Greek φλόξ (phlox) comes from a root that evokes the movement and brilliance of fire. In Hebrew, the main word translated is לַהַב (lahab), which designates both the visible flame and the bright glow of fire. The Greek word φλόξ carries the primitive image of fire as something that "flies" or "rises" — a fiery, living tongue that does not stay in place. This image of fire that rises and shines naturally, the Bible will use to evoke the presence and power of God.
G5395.emploi: The word flame appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles and Revelation. Luke uses it only once, in the parable of the rich man and the poor man, to describe the concrete experience of punishment. Acts uses it for the burning bush, a classic theophany of the Old Testament. The epistle to the Hebrews and especially Revelation give the word its major theological significance: the flame becomes an attribute of divinity, a sign of judgment and the omniscience of the risen Christ. It is particularly in John's visions that flame takes on all its symbolic weight, closely linked with fire, purity, and divine justice.
G5395.portee: Understanding that the flame, for John and the early Christians, is not primarily an image of punishment, but a sign of the living and present divinity. The "eyes like a flame of fire" of the glorified Christ remind the reader that nothing escapes his knowledge, and that this light reveals both love and judgment. It is an invitation to respect the real and penetrating presence of the risen Christ in the life of the Church.

sens: Speak against someone by uttering malicious and senseless words
Accuse or slander with hollow and wicked words
G5396.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of someone who speaks ill of another person — not by making founded criticisms, but by spitting out wicked words, often devoid of meaning or unjust. It is more than simple gossip: it is to attack someone with words. In 3 John 10, Diotrephes "speaks wicked words against us": he creates a hostile atmosphere with his malicious words.
2. The word also suggests a certain irresponsibility in speech: one says things without solid foundation, just to hurt or to dominate. The one who acts this way does not seek the truth; he seeks to destroy reputation or peace. It is an abuse of speech, used as a weapon.
G5396.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek φλύαρος (phluaros), which means first "verbose, talkative," then "speaking for no reason" or "speaking senselessly." The root evokes the idea of futile, empty, or deceptive words. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, the idea is close to מרמה (mirmah), deception by speech, or דברי־שפחה (words of a servant), that is, words without weight or truth.
G5396.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 3 John 10, where it characterizes the behavior of Diotrephes. John does not describe Diotrephes as simply disagreeing or critical: he presents him as someone who sows discord through aggressive and unfounded words. This rare and incisive term marks the seriousness of the problem: malicious speech is not a mere flaw, it is a threat to the Church.
G5396.portee: This word warns us against the abuse of speech. Speaking injuriously against our brothers is serious: it distorts the truth, hurts without reason, and creates an atmosphere of fear and distrust. For the Christian, this reminds us that our speech must be true, loving, and constructive — never a weapon to dominate or destroy.

sens: Who speaks a lot, without restraint or measure
Who chatters, spreads idle or malicious words
Prone to frivolity and sterile chatter
G5397.detail:
1. A person who constantly talks, not knowing when to be silent. The word evokes someone who lets their tongue go freely, without control. In 1 Timothy 5:13, Paul describes widows who become "gossips and busybodies," unable to keep silent.
2. Beyond simple chatter, it involves words that hurt or disturb: one reports what one has heard, spreads gossip. These words are presented as "what should not be said."
3. It is a disposition of the soul: the one who is a gossip finds pleasure in talking for the sake of talking, rather than reflecting or acting usefully. Idleness and chatter go hand in hand in the Pauline passage.
G5397.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to babble" or "to stammer" — an imitation of the vain noise of words. It describes less someone who talks a lot because they have something to say, than someone who talks because their mouth cannot stop. It is a colorful, slightly contemptuous word that evokes superficial chatter rather than serious speech.
G5397.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:13. Paul uses it to describe the spiritual danger that threatens young widows who remain inactive and idle: they become not only gossips but also "busybodies" who spread malicious remarks. The context shows that chronic chatter is linked to idleness and the absence of useful occupation. Paul presents this as a serious moral weakness, hence his insistence that younger widows remarry and take care of their homes.
G5397.portee: This word invites the Christian to watch over their tongue and their time: constant chatter reveals a restless and empty soul, and can harm others. For those who feel inclined to talk incessantly, it is a call to cultivate silence, reflection, and useful action. For all, it is a reminder that our words matter and that we will be held accountable for them.

sens: That inspires fear, dread, anxiety
That fills with fright, apprehension
G5398.detail:
1. This word describes what provokes fear, dread, what is formidable and impressive due to its power or gravity. In Hebrews 10:27, Paul speaks of a "terrible expectation of judgment": the idea of divine judgment fills the unbelievers with terror. In Hebrews 10:31, "to fall into the hands of the living God" is a terrible thing, a fate that makes one shudder. It is the dread before the power and holiness of God.
2. The word can also describe the state of one who feels this fear: in Hebrews 12:21, Moses is seized with terror before God's manifestation at Sinai, to the point of saying, "I am terrified and trembling." It is then the inner effect of what is imposing and transcendent.
G5398.origine: The word comes from the verb "phobéô" (to fear, to be afraid). It designates what provokes fear or one who is seized by it. In classical Greek, it is related to other terms meaning "formidable" or "timid," depending on the context. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it generally translates the Hebrew "yaré" (to fear, to be afraid), which is the fundamental reaction before the holiness of God.
G5398.emploi: The word appears only three times in Greek in the New Testament, solely in the Epistle to the Hebrews. It is always in the active sense: what causes fear. In Hebrews 10:27 and 10:31, it qualifies divine judgment and God's justice, which should inspire respect and fear in those who ignore them. In Hebrews 12:21, it describes the terrifying atmosphere of the theophany at Sinai, the moment when God manifested Himself to the people through superhuman signs. The author of the Epistle uses this word to emphasize the formidable nature of God and the gravity of judgment.
G5398.portee: This word invites us to understand God's holiness and justice, not as abstract concepts, but as terrifying and formidable for those who confront them without faith. The "fear of God" is not cowardice, but a rightful acknowledgment of His power and authority: it is a reality that everyone must take seriously. For the believer, it calls for vigilance and respect towards the one who can judge; for the unbeliever, it announces a terrible fate. This word reminds us that the Christian faith does not evade divine judgment, but traverses it through the grace of Christ.

sens: To be afraid, to be seized with fright in the face of danger or the unknown
To dread something or someone, to apprehend the consequences
To deeply respect someone due to their authority or power
To have reverence towards God
G5399.detail:
1. Natural fear: it is the fright that seizes someone in the face of an event that surprises or threatens them. When the angel appears to the women at the tomb, he says to them, "Do not be afraid" (Matthew 28:5); when the disciples see Jesus walking on the water, they are afraid thinking He is a ghost (Mark 6:50).
2. Apprehension: it is to dread an unfavorable outcome. The apostle Paul fears that he has labored in vain for the Galatians (Galatians 4:11), meaning he is concerned about the result of his preaching.
3. Fearful respect towards an authority: one fears someone because they recognize them as superior and dread their reaction. The religious leaders feared Jesus because the crowd supported Him (Mark 11:18).
4. Reverence towards God: it is a religious respect, a mixture of love and respectful apprehension. Scripture speaks of men "who fear God" (Acts 13:16) as an honorable designation for those who cling to the Lord.
G5399.origine: The word φοβέω comes from φόβος (fear, fright). In Hebrew, it primarily translates יָרֵא (yéra), which means to be afraid but also to honor or venerate. This dual dimension—fear in the face of danger and respect in the presence of the powerful—is present throughout biblical history: we fear God, but we can also fear Him with love. The family of the word also includes φόβος (fear itself) and other forms related to fright.
G5399.emploi: The verb appears about 92 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. The uses are distributed into three categories: natural fear (disciples and witnesses of marvelous events), apprehension of an unfavorable consequence (Paul fears that his work may be in vain), and respect or fear towards an authority (fear of God, of rulers, of religious leaders). The passive form predominates significantly ("to be feared") and the context determines whether the fear is justified or to be overcome. Jesus often addresses this fear: "do not be afraid" is a word of comfort He addresses to His own.
G5399.portee: For the Christian reader, this word marks the importance of a proper attitude towards what exceeds humanity. Jesus eliminates the paralyzing fear of the believer but invites to cultivate the fear of God—not through terror, but through a loving reverence towards the Father. Understanding the nuances of this word helps to live without anxiety in the face of circumstances, while maintaining a constant reverence before the Lord.

sens: recipient or trough where animal food is placed
the resting place of the newborn Jesus
G5336.detail:
1. A manger is primarily a trough or bin, usually made of stone or wood, where fodder or food for domestic animals (oxen, donkeys, horses) is placed. It is a utilitarian piece of furniture found on a farm or in a stable. In Luke 13:15, Jesus speaks of one who "unties his ox or donkey from the manger to lead it to drink" on the Sabbath—these are the feeding troughs for the animals.
2. The manger becomes famous in the Gospel as the humble cradle where Mary laid the newborn Jesus: "she wrapped him and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn" (Luke 2:7). The shepherds find the child "lying in a manger" (Luke 2:16). This detail emphasizes the poverty and humility of the Savior's birthplace.
G5336.origine: The Greek word φάτνη comes from a root that evokes the action of putting or placing. It likely relates to the idea of fixing or establishing firmly. The Hebrew word אֵבוּס (ēbus) that the Greek version of the Old Testament translates by this term also refers to the trough or feeding place. It is a simple word, part of the everyday vocabulary of rural and pastoral life in the Near East.
G5336.emploi: The word appears only 4 times in the New Testament, all in Luke. Three times (Luke 2:7, 2:12, 2:16), it is found in the account of Jesus' birth in Bethlehem, where the manger is the detail that makes the humility of this event concrete and touching. A fourth time (Luke 13:15), Jesus uses it as an example in a controversy about the Sabbath: a man unties his livestock from the manger to water them, an act of mercy that cannot be refused on the Sabbath, especially towards a human being. The word is always very concrete, rooted in ordinary life.
G5336.portee: The manger where the newborn Jesus rests is not a picturesque detail: it is a powerful image of the incarnation and the voluntary humility of the Son of God. The one who created the worlds is born in a stable, resting in an animal trough. This humble and raw reality teaches the believer that God accepted the simplest and poorest conditions to enter into relationship with humanity.

sens: What is bad, contrary to good
What is worthless, despicable
What is morally reprehensible or guilty
What causes disorder or confusion
G5337.detail:
1. Evil primarily refers to any bad act or behavior, the direct opposite of good. In John 3:20, the one who "does evil" flees from the light because his works are condemnable; in John 5:29, resurrecting "for evil" means resurrecting to be judged, not for life. It is the morally reprehensible action in its concrete reality.

2. The word also expresses what is unimportant, despicable, or futile. Although less apparent in these usages in the New Testament, this nuance can be inferred when contrasting "good" and "evil" in terms of value: doing evil is doing what has no value in the eyes of God.

3. On a moral and spiritual level, evil qualifies what opposes the will and holiness of God. In Romans 9:11, being accused of having done "evil" falls under divine judgment. In 2 Corinthians 5:10, everyone will answer before the judgment seat of Christ for what they have done "evil" during their earthly life—this word evokes the moral responsibility of each person.

4. Evil can also mean disorder, disturbance, that which breaks peace. James 3:16 speaks of "all kinds of evil actions" where bitter jealousy and strife reign: evil is then the natural fruit of spiritual and emotional chaos.
G5337.origine: The Greek word φαῦλος comes from an ancient root and etymologically designates what is weak, thin, of little value. It does not carry the idea of active malice, but rather that of a moral failing: an absence of good rather than malignity. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew עֶוֶל ("injustice") and אֱוִיל ("foolishness"), showing that evil, in Hebrew as in Greek, is often linked to the foolish and the wicked. The word remained common in Greek philosophy, where it designated what is vain or futile, but the New Testament always uses it with an explicit moral charge.
G5337.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, spread across four books: three times in the Gospels (John), twice in the Pauline epistles (Romans, 2 Corinthians), once in the pastoral epistle (Titus), and once in the epistle of James. In John 3:20 and 5:29, it refers to the evil works of the human heart and actions worthy of judgment. In Romans 9:11, it opposes "good" to express that no work, good or evil, can justify before God. In 2 Corinthians 5:10, it evokes moral responsibility at the final judgment. In Titus 2:8, "having nothing evil to say about us" takes on a slightly different shade: evil as reproach or accusation. In James 3:16, it expresses the disorder and confusion produced by a quarrelsome spirit. The range of usages shows that evil, in the New Testament, is always a moral reality, never neutral: it is what offends God and deserves judgment.
G5337.portee: This word reminds the believer that their actions have an absolute moral significance: there are no neutral or insignificant acts in the eyes of God. Every "evil" we commit, every injustice, every breach of peace, will be examined at the judgment seat of Christ. But at the same time, the New Testament always places evil in contrast to good, inviting the Christian to consciously choose: to flee the darkness of evil and walk in the light, as John 3:20 says. It is a call to vigilance and personal moral responsibility.

sens: Brightness, radiance emitted or reflected by a star or light source
Glow of a celestial body shining in the sky
G5338.detail:
1. This word designates the brightness or luminous radiance that emanates from a source—the sun, the moon, a lamp—or that is reflected from it. It is the visible, concrete light that allows us to see. In Matthew 24:29, Jesus announces that "the moon will not give its light anymore": he speaks of this palpable radiance that we see in the night sky.
2. The word is particularly used for the glow of celestial bodies. In Mark 13:24, in the same eschatological discourse, the moon ceases to give its light—the celestial body loses its brightness. The image is that of a celestial source that is extinguished or disappears.
G5338.origine: The Greek word phengos comes from a root that evokes the idea of shining, glowing. It belongs to the same family of words as other Greek terms designating light or radiance. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew nogah, which means "splendor" or "brilliant radiance." It is a concrete and vivid word: it always refers to visible, tangible light, never abstract.
G5338.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in eschatological contexts—that is, in the description of the signs of the end times. Matthew 24:29 and Mark 13:24 parallel it in Jesus' warning discourse: at the final judgment, the stars will lose their brightness. The use of the word shows that the Bible speaks here of the physical light that the stars send us, not of an abstract spiritual reality. The apocalyptic context gives the word a dramatic charge: natural light is extinguished, symbolizing cosmic rupture.
G5338.portee: This word invites reflection on the fragility of natural realities that seem immutable to us—the sun, the moon—and on the fact that only divine authority can stop their course. For the believer, it emphasizes that the end of the world will not be a mere cosmic event, but the fulfillment of the divine plan. It is also a call not to place trust in the stars or visible realities, but in the one who governs them.
